name: RegistryGuard
one_liner: Monitors a govcon's SAM.gov entity registration, exclusion status, and teaming partners' registrations, and fires deadline-math alerts (60/30/15/1-day) before lapse cuts off contract eligibility.
problem: SAM.gov registrations expire exactly 365 days after approval; SAM.gov's own reminder emails go to a single Electronic Business POC and are routinely missed when that person leaves or the email lands in spam, causing payment stoppages of 60-90 days and loss of bid eligibility (fedbizaccess.com/govdash/capturepilot 2026 guides, fetched 2026-08-19). A live third-party API already sells exactly this expiration-check feature standalone at $39/mo Pro tier, 1,000 req/hr (govconapi.com/sam-registration-expiration-checker, fetched 2026-08-19), proving a paying market exists for a bare API — a polished multi-entity monitoring product with dashboards/alerts for compliance officers and BD teams (who must also track subcontractor/teaming-partner registration status, not just their own) is a clear upsell on that same willingness to pay.
target_customer: Small-to-mid federal contractors (5-200 employees) and the compliance/BD staff at govcon primes who must track their own SAM registration plus subcontractor/teaming-partner registrations and exclusion status before award.
evidence: Live pain: SAM registrations lapse and cause 60-90 day payment stoppages per multiple 2026 govcon guides. Live paid comparable: GovCon API sells the identical expiration-check endpoint standalone at $39/mo (fetched https://govconapi.com/sam-registration-expiration-checker on 2026-08-19).
knowledge_base: api.sam.gov Entity Management API (public GET endpoints at https://api.sam.gov/entity-information/v3/entities, confirmed live via https://open.gsa.gov/api/entity-api/ fetched 2026-08-19) returns registrationExpirationDate, UEI, exclusion flags, NAICS/PSC per entity; refreshed by SAM.gov continuously as registrants renew, polled on a daily cron per tracked UEI. Staleness is self-detecting: if a UEI's registrationExpirationDate in our cache falls in the past relative to the API's current record, or the API call itself fails/returns stale ETag, the cron flags the record for re-fetch before the next alert cycle runs.
autonomy_case: A1: signup/payment/UEI-list entry all self-serve, Stripe billing, no sales call needed to add a UEI to watch. A2: alerts are pure deterministic date arithmetic (expirationDate - today vs threshold) against API JSON — no human review of any output. A3: when the SAM API is unreachable or a UEI record is malformed, the product just shows 'last known status as of [date], re-checking' rather than guessing or routing to a person. A4: api.sam.gov is public, machine-readable, updated continuously by GSA; cron polls daily and detects staleness via HTTP status/ETag. A5: polling, alert-sending (email/webhook), and billing dunning are all cron jobs with retry/fail-closed (alert 'could not verify status' rather than silently skipping). A6: no per-customer human touch — adding/removing a UEI is self-service in the dashboard; support load is bounded because the only variable input is a UEI number, not bespoke integration work.
moat: Aggregation across many tracked entities (a prime tracking 40 subs) plus historical lapse/renewal pattern data becomes harder to replicate than a single-UEI lookup API; switching cost rises with the number of saved UEIs and alert-routing rules (Slack/email/webhook per team).
pricing_hypothesis: $49-99/mo per account for up to 25 tracked UEIs (self + subs/teaming partners), with a higher tier for 100+ UEIs aimed at primes/PTACs managing many subcontractors — anchored just above the existing $39/mo bare-API comparable since this adds multi-entity dashboards and routed alerts.
revenue_model: Monthly SaaS subscription tiered by number of tracked UEIs, self-serve Stripe checkout, auto-renewal, auto-dunning on card failure.
time_to_first_revenue: 2-3 weeks (API integration + Stripe + basic alert engine is a small, well-scoped build against a documented, already-live API).
risks: api.sam.gov's low free-tier rate limit (10 req/day for unpermissioned non-federal users, 1,000/day with a role per open.gsa.gov docs fetched 2026-08-19) may require applying for a higher-throughput system account as the tracked-UEI count grows — need to verify actual account-tier request early. Incumbent govconapi.com could bundle a dashboard itself and commoditize the wrapper. Not yet verified: exact conversion economics from free SAM.gov reminder emails to paid third-party monitoring (i.e., how many contractors are wiling to pay when SAM sends free reminders already) — worth a landing-page test before build.
why_simple: One polling job (GET registration status per tracked UEI), one comparison (expiration date vs thresholds), one alert dispatcher (email/webhook) — no ML, no document generation, no case-specific judgment calls.

name: Form4Clock
one_liner: Watches EDGAR Form 3/4/5 filings for a company's designated insiders and computes exact SEC 2-business-day filing deadlines (with federal holiday calendar), flagging any filing that is late or about to be late before the plaintiffs' bar or SEC exam sweep finds it.
problem: Form 4 must be filed within two business days of an insider transaction, and this is 'the most commonly missed deadline in Section 16 compliance' because insiders trade without notifying the compliance team same-day (finrep.ai 2026 practitioner guide, fetched 2026-08-19). Late filings create two live financial consequences with money already changing hands to avoid them: (1) shareholder plaintiffs' firms actively scan Form 4 filings specifically hunting short-swing-profit (Section 16(b)) disgorgement suits, taking 20-30% contingency fees on recovered profits (acquisitionstars.com, fetched 2026-08-19), and (2) the SEC can pursue civil penalties/cease-and-desist orders for delinquent-filer patterns found in exam sweeps, and late filers must be named in the company's own DEF 14A under Item 405 — a public reputational cost. Existing paid Section 16 filing/compliance software (e.g., Form345.com) already serves this market as a distinct software category.
target_customer: In-house securities/compliance counsel and corporate secretaries at small-and-mid-cap public companies (where compliance headcount is thin and Form 4 tracking is manual/spreadsheet-based) who are personally on the hook if their insiders file late.
evidence: Live confirmed deadline-math pain from a 2026 practitioner guide (finrep.ai, fetched 2026-08-19) and confirmed litigation-economics driver: plaintiffs' firms scan Form 4 specifically for Section 16(b) short-swing suits with 20-30% contingency (acquisitionstars.com, fetched 2026-08-19). A standalone commercial Section 16 filing-software category already exists and is marketed on this exact pain (form345.com/filing-form-4, page confirmed live though pricing not extractable due to 403 on fetch, fetched 2026-08-19).
knowledge_base: SEC EDGAR company-specific Form 3/4/5 atom feed (https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=...&type=4&output=atom — confirmed live 2026-08-19, returned real filing-date 2026-08-13 for Apple Inc. CIK 0000320193) plus the underlying per-filing structured XML (transactionDate field in the Form 4 document) and data.sec.gov/submissions/CIK##########.json (confirmed live 2026-08-19) for issuer/insider linkage. Refresh: EDGAR is updated in near-real time as filings are accepted; cron polls each tracked issuer's feed on an hourly cadence during market hours, and staleness is self-detecting because each feed entry carries its own accession-number/filing-date that must monotonically advance — a stalled feed (no new entries when trading volume data elsewhere shows activity) triggers a 'last verified as of' banner rather than a silent gap.
autonomy_case: A1: company signs up, adds CIK + list of insider names/roles, pays via Stripe, no sales call. A2: the entire output is deterministic — business-day countdown from a transaction date parsed out of structured XML, compared against a fixed federal holiday calendar (also public, from OPM), rendered as a red/amber/green countdown per insider; no generative step in the compliance-critical number. A3: if a Form 4's transactionDate field is missing or a filing type is ambiguous, the product shows 'transaction date not machine-parseable, verify manually' next to that one filing rather than guessing a deadline or paging a human reviewer — it degrades per-filing, not company-wide. A4: EDGAR filings are the public system of record itself, refreshed continuously, no manual curation. A5: polling, deadline computation, and email/Slack alert dispatch are all cron-schedulable with retry. A6: zero human minutes per customer after setup — the only variable input per customer is their own CIK and insider list, not a bespoke workflow.
moat: Per-issuer historical delinquency tracking (useful for that DEF 14A Item 405 disclosure prep) and multi-insider dashboards compound in value the longer a company stays subscribed; also a natural adjacent expansion into Form 13F/13D deadline tracking for the same buyer persona.
pricing_hypothesis: $150-400/mo per issuer (priced against legal/reputational risk avoidance, not against cheap consumer tools) — anchored below what a single missed Section 16(b) contingency suit or SEC penalty would cost, and comparable to existing Section 16 filing-software subscriptions.
revenue_model: Monthly SaaS per tracked issuer/CIK, self-serve signup and card billing, tiered by number of insiders tracked.
time_to_first_revenue: 3-4 weeks (EDGAR polling + XML parsing for transactionDate + business-day calendar math is bounded, well-documented public data).
risks: Form345.com pricing could not be verified live (403 on fetch) — must confirm actual price point before anchoring; if it's a free/bundled feature of a larger transfer-agent suite rather than a standalone paid product, the 'worse solution people pay for' evidence weakens and needs a second comparable (e.g., Broadridge/DFIN Section 16 module pricing) before committing. Buyer is a company/compliance officer, not the individual insider — need to confirm this is not effectively enterprise-sales-only (larger issuers may expect a demo before adopting compliance-critical software), which could pressure A1/A6 at the higher end of the market.
why_simple: Two dates (transaction date, filing date), one calendar (federal holidays), one comparison — the entire deliverable is a countdown timer and a red/green flag, no natural-language generation of the compliance-bearing number.

name: RecompeteRadar
one_liner: Computes and alerts on federal contract period-of-performance end dates by NAICS/agency/set-aside so small govcon bizdev teams get a recompete pipeline without paying five-figure GovWin IQ fees.
problem: Deltek's GovWin IQ, the incumbent tool for tracking upcoming federal contract recompetes, runs $12,000-42,000/year with an average deal near $29,000/year (Vendr data via civiciq.com, fetched 2026-08-19) and requires a sales call with no self-serve signup or published pricing (fed-spend.com, fetched 2026-08-19) — explicitly locking out any business whose 'annual federal contract intelligence budget is below $10,000' per that same 2026 comparison piece. A direct competitor (Fed-Spend) already sells a cheaper self-serve alternative at $39-199/mo and markets itself as '68x cheaper than GovWin,' which is itself live proof both that money changes hands for this exact use case and that GovWin's price point is considered a solvable pain point worth building a company around.
target_customer: Small business federal contractors (under $20M revenue) and 1-3 person bizdev/capture teams who need to know when their agency's contracts in their NAICS codes are coming up for recompete, but cannot justify GovWin IQ's enterprise price and sales cycle.
evidence: Live-fetched pricing: GovWin IQ $12k-42k/yr, avg ~$29k/yr (civiciq.com blog, fetched 2026-08-19); live-fetched competitor pricing proving the underserved segment already pays for a cheaper alternative: Fed-Spend Researcher tier $588/yr, Professional tier $1,908-2,388/yr (fed-spend.com, fetched 2026-08-19).
knowledge_base: USAspending.gov Award Search API, https://api.usaspending.gov/api/v2/search/spending_by_award/ — confirmed live and free with no authentication required ('Endpoints do not currently require any authorization' per official docs, fetched 2026-08-19) via a live test query on 2026-08-19 that returned real contract records with Start Date/End Date/Award Amount/Recipient fields (e.g. CACI-ISS LLC contract W15QKN15C0049, End Date 2025-06-02). Refreshed daily by the Treasury/USASpending pipeline from FPDS submissions; staleness is self-detecting because each award record carries its own last-modified data and the /api/v2/references/... status endpoints expose pipeline load dates that a daily cron checks before trusting a pull.
autonomy_case: A1: self-serve signup, pick NAICS/agency/set-aside filters, pay by card, no sales call, no demo. A2: the product is a computed, filtered, sorted list of contracts whose period-of-performance end date falls in a configurable window (e.g., next 6-18 months) — generated entirely by querying and filtering structured API fields, zero human curation of the list. A3: when a specific award's End Date field is null or a NAICS code is missing (which occurred in the live test query above), the product shows that record flagged 'incomplete government data — end date not reported' rather than guessing or omitting it silently, and narrows confidence rather than escalating to a person. A4: USASpending API is the public system of record, refreshed continuously from FPDS; cron pulls daily per saved filter set. A5: polling, filter-matching, and alert/digest emails are all cron-schedulable with retry and fail-closed logging. A6: zero human minutes per customer — the only customer input is a saved filter (NAICS/agency/set-aside/dollar range), not a bespoke research request.
moat: Saved-filter alert history and a growing per-agency/per-NAICS recompete calendar becomes a compounding dataset asset; multi-year win-rate context (which incumbents tend to get recompeted vs re-bid) deepens with tenure, raising switching cost.
pricing_hypothesis: $79-249/mo tiered by number of saved NAICS/agency filter sets and alert frequency — priced well under Fed-Spend's Professional tier ($159-199/mo) by staying narrowly focused on recompete-deadline alerting rather than full award-search/BI, while still capturing the segment GovWin excludes.
revenue_model: Monthly SaaS subscription, self-serve Stripe signup, tiered by number of tracked filter sets/agencies, auto-renew with card-failure dunning.
time_to_first_revenue: 3-4 weeks (USASpending API is already confirmed live, documented, and free; the build is filter-management UI plus a daily cron digest).
risks: NAICS Code came back null in several live test records for this exact contract type, meaning field completeness varies by agency/contract action and the product must handle gaps transparently (already reflected in the A3 degrade behavior) rather than presenting false precision. Competitive crowding: Fed-Spend and Civic IQ already occupy the 'cheap GovWin alternative' positioning broadly — this idea's differentiation must stay narrow (recompete-deadline alerting specifically, not general award search/BI) or it becomes a me-too. Not yet verified live: actual small-business willingness to pay specifically for a recompete-alert-only product versus a full search tool — worth testing narrow pricing before building a broad feature set.
why_simple: Filter awards by NAICS/agency/set-aside, sort by period-of-performance end date, email a digest when a date crosses into the alert window — no generative writing, no proposal drafting, just structured-field filtering and date math.

name: Chameleon Carrier Screen
one_liner: Point-in-time fraud/identity screening API for freight brokers and factoring underwriters, built entirely from deterministic red-flag rules run against FMCSA's public carrier registration, insurance, and safety files.
problem: Before tendering a load or funding an invoice, brokers and factors must know whether a motor carrier is a legitimate, insured operator or a 'chameleon' carrier (freshly re-authorized after a revocation, insurance added days before pickup, address/officer overlap with a previously flagged MC number). The Transportation Intermediaries Association's fraud estimate and FMCSA's own complaint volume show this is a fast-growing, expensive problem, and multiple paid tools already exist to solve exactly this with public government data, none of them AI-generative — they run rules against SAFER/L&I fields.
target_customer: Small-to-mid freight brokerages (2-50 employees) and freight-factoring underwriting teams who currently do manual SAFER lookups or pay for existing carrier-monitoring seats.
evidence: Money already changes hands for this exact category: SaferWatch charges $79.95/mo for carrier research + watchlist monitoring (fetched https://truckbrokerinsurancenetwork.gtu-ins.com/why-we-and-you-should-use-saferwatch-for-carrier-selection/ and corroborating search result, 2026-08-19). VerifyCarrier publishes tiered pricing $19-$99/mo for API lookups and a 'Broker/Broker Pro/Platform' monitoring product at $49-$249/mo (fetched https://verifycarrier.com/pricing, 2026-08-19). Carrier411 charges per-seat (third-party estimate ~$34.95/user/mo per https://verifycarrier.com/vs/carrier-411, fetched 2026-08-19 — flagged as a secondary estimate, not Carrier411's own published number). TIA estimates double-brokering/fraud costs the industry $700M-$1B/yr and FMCSA complaint volume rose from ~2,000 (2021) to 8,000+ (2025) (per search-aggregated coverage of truckinginfo.com/authenticate.com, 2026-08-19 — flagged as secondary reporting, worth re-verifying against FMCSA's own numbers before build). A dedicated factoring-fraud product, 'Freight Shield' by Decipher Credit, exists as further proof of willingness to pay in the factoring-underwriting sub-segment (https://deciphercredit.com/freight-shield-combating-factoring-fraud-in-trucking/, fetched 2026-08-19).
knowledge_base: FMCSA QCMobile API (https://mobile.fmcsa.dot.gov/qc/services/carriers/{dotNumber}/basics — free ad-hoc JSON snapshot, confirmed live via docs at https://mobile.fmcsa.dot.gov/QCDevsite/docs/qcApi, fetched 2026-08-19) for real-time authority/insurance/safety-rating status; FMCSA Licensing & Insurance bulk Socrata datasets on data.transportation.gov — Carrier file (6eyk-hxee), Active & Pending Insurance (qh9u-swkp), Authority History (9mw4-x3tu) — confirmed to exist via catalog.data.gov listing (fetched 2026-08-19, page render was sparse so exact refresh cadence needs direct Socrata metadata confirmation before build) for detecting newly-granted or reinstated authority; FMCSA SMS monthly bulk census/inspection/crash files at https://ai.fmcsa.dot.gov/SMS/Tools/Downloads.aspx, posted to data.gov by the 15th of the following month per catalog.data.gov description (fetched 2026-08-19), for CSA BASIC percentiles. Staleness is detectable because each Socrata/SMS file carries its own last-updated/vintage field.
autonomy_case: A1: signup + Stripe metered/subscription billing, no sales call — pricing pages of direct comps (VerifyCarrier) show this is already sold self-serve. A2: the fraud score is a deterministic rule engine (days-since-authority-granted, insurance-added-in-last-N-days, revoked-MC address/officer match, no active BMC-91 filing) computed purely from structured government fields — no review queue. A3: when a data field is missing or a match is ambiguous, the product states 'insufficient public data to score as of [date]' rather than guessing, and a low-confidence result narrows to the specific missing field. A4: nightly cron pulls QCMobile snapshots on demand plus monthly SMS/Socrata refreshes; a dataset with a stale 'last updated' timestamp flips the UI to a staleness banner automatically. A5: ingestion, scoring, alerting and dunning are all schedulable jobs with no human step. A6: support load is bounded because the product only ever answers 'what do the government files say and when were they last confirmed,' never a judgment call requiring a human underwriter.
moat: Not a moat in the defensible-technology sense — the data is public and several well-funded competitors already exist (SaferWatch, VerifyCarrier, Carrier411, CarrierOK). The wedge is being cheaper/simpler self-serve API-first pricing for the long tail of very small brokerages and factoring shops that VerifyCarrier's own free/starter tiers show is underserved, plus a narrower focus on the fraud-recency signals (newly granted authority, insurance-just-added) that generalist snapshot tools bury.
pricing_hypothesis: $0 up to N free lookups/mo, then $29-$99/mo for a monitored watchlist of 25-250 carriers, mirroring VerifyCarrier's confirmed $19-$99 API tiers and $49-$249 monitoring tiers.
revenue_model: Tiered SaaS subscription by watchlist size + metered API overage, Stripe self-serve.
time_to_first_revenue: 2-4 weeks: QCMobile is free and keyless for ad-hoc queries, so a thin MVP (single-carrier score + email alert) can ship before the bulk-file ingestion pipeline is fully built.
risks: Not yet verified: FMCSA's own primary fraud-loss and complaint-count figures (currently sourced from secondary trade coverage, not FMCSA.gov directly) — must re-pull from FMCSA's public statistics before using in marketing copy. Also unverified: exact Socrata refresh cadence for the three L&I bulk files (page did not render field-level metadata on fetch) and whether QCMobile's free ad-hoc tier has an undocumented rate limit at scale. Competitive intensity is real — this is a crowded category, so the product must win on price/simplicity, not on data exclusivity.
why_simple: No LLM in the decision path: every flag is a boolean/threshold test against a government-published field (authority grant date, insurance filing date, revocation history). The model, if used at all, only writes the plain-English explanation of a rule that already fired.
persona: Ex-carrier-sales-rep-turned-solo-SaaS-builder who knows FMCSA's data model cold and wants a narrow, boring, high-trust compliance tool.

name: Recall Clear
one_liner: Automated open-recall inventory scanning and dated disclosure-certificate generation for used-car dealers, BHPH lots, auto auctions and repossession lienholders, built entirely on NHTSA's free VIN-decode and recall APIs.
problem: Selling or auctioning a used vehicle with an undisclosed open safety recall creates real legal and financial exposure for dealers and lienholders, and checking a whole lot's VINs one-by-one on NHTSA.gov is slow and easy to skip.
target_customer: Independent used-car dealers, buy-here-pay-here lots, small auto auctions, and bank/credit-union teams disposing of repossessed vehicles who cannot afford or qualify for enterprise DMS-bundled recall add-ons.
evidence: This exact exposure already produced a real cash settlement: Massachusetts AG announced a $1M multistate settlement with CarMax over failure to disclose safety recalls, requiring CarMax to present open-recall copies and obtain signed disclosures before sale (https://www.mass.gov/news/ag-healey-announces-1-million-multistate-settlement-with-carmax-over-failure-to-disclose-safety-recalls, fetched 2026-08-19). Consumer groups also sued the FTC over allowing 'certified pre-owned' labeling on recalled cars (https://www.nbcnews.com/business/consumer/ftc-sued-allowing-car-dealers-sell-recalled-vehicles-potentially-lethal-defects-n720276, referenced via search 2026-08-19). Paid automated incumbents already serve this exact workflow: AutoAp's Dealer Recall Management / API modules (Verify, Monitor, Campaign, Disclose) claim manual VIN-by-VIN recall monitoring can cost a dealership '$40,000 or more annually' before automation (per autosuccessonline.com / autodealertodaymagazine.com coverage of AutoAp's own product materials, fetched via search 2026-08-19 — AutoAp's own subscription price was not published and needs direct confirmation), and a consumer-grade competitor, Your Service Book, publishes subscription pricing of $2.99-$10/mo (per search result, 2026-08-19), showing a price floor for VIN-level recall tracking exists even at the individual-vehicle level.
knowledge_base: NHTSA vPIC API for VIN decoding — confirmed free, keyless, JSON/XML/CSV, batch endpoint for up to 50 VINs at a time (https://vpic.nhtsa.dot.gov/api/, fetched live 2026-08-19). NHTSA Recalls API for open-campaign lookup by make/model/year — confirmed live and keyless by direct fetch of https://api.nhtsa.gov/recalls/recallsByVehicle?make=honda&model=accord&modelYear=2018 (fetched 2026-08-19), returning structured fields (NHTSACampaignNumber, Component, Summary, Consequence, Remedy, ReportReceivedDate, parkIt/overTheAirUpdate flags). Staleness is detectable per-query since each recall record carries its own ReportReceivedDate and campaign number that can be diffed against the prior nightly pull.
autonomy_case: A1: dealer self-signs-up, uploads a VIN list or CSV export from their existing inventory system, pays by Stripe — no onboarding call needed since the only integration is a CSV/VIN paste. A2: fulfilment is pure code — VIN decode, then recall lookup by decoded make/model/year, then templated PDF generation; nothing is reviewed by a person. A3: when a VIN can't be decoded or a recall record is ambiguous, the output says 'no open NHTSA campaign found as of [date]' with the exact query parameters shown, rather than asserting a compliance guarantee — this is a narrowed, sourced claim, not a human escalation. A4: nightly cron re-queries the full inventory against the recall API and diffs against yesterday's snapshot; a failed/empty API response flips the dashboard to a staleness warning automatically. A5: ingestion, PDF generation, and email alerts are all cron-schedulable and fail closed (no PDF issued if the API call errors). A6: support load is bounded to 're-run the check' since there is no manual research step ever required.
moat: Thin on data (NHTSA's API is open to anyone, including AutoAp and Recall Masters) — the edge is serving the long tail of small/independent dealers and lienholders that AutoAp's enterprise/DMS-integration sales motion likely does not reach at self-serve prices, plus positioning the output specifically as a signed, dated legal-disclosure artifact (mirroring exactly what the CarMax settlement required) rather than a generic dashboard.
pricing_hypothesis: $49-$199/mo tiered by inventory size (e.g., up to 50 / 200 / unlimited VINs), undercutting the enterprise DMS-bundled recall add-ons and roughly at or below AutoAp's implied value claim (avoiding a claimed $40k/yr manual cost).
revenue_model: Flat monthly SaaS subscription by inventory size, self-serve Stripe billing, annual discount.
time_to_first_revenue: 1-3 weeks: both underlying NHTSA APIs are free, keyless and already fetched live in this research, so a VIN-paste MVP producing a PDF disclosure sheet can ship almost immediately.
risks: AutoAp's own subscription pricing was not directly confirmed (only its cost-avoidance marketing claim was found) and should be re-verified before positioning against it. The NHTSA recall API matches by make/model/year, not directly by VIN, so edge cases (mid-year running changes, VIN-specific campaigns) need careful handling to avoid false negatives — a real defensibility/liability risk if the product mis-states 'no open recall.' Legal-disclosure-document generation should be reviewed for state-specific language requirements (e.g., what CarMax's settlement required) even though the fulfilment itself stays code-only.
why_simple: No generative step in the compliance claim: the AI, if used at all, only formats the PDF disclosure layout — whether a recall applies is a direct API match against NHTSA's own structured campaign data, keyed on decoded VIN attributes.
persona: Auto-industry ops person who has seen dealer recall-disclosure liability firsthand and wants a cheap, boring compliance tool for independent lots that enterprise DMS vendors ignore.

name: Carrier Continuity Watch
one_liner: A standing monitor (not a one-time lookup) that alerts freight brokers and factoring companies the moment a carrier already in their approved network lapses on UCR, BOC-3, or cargo/liability insurance — the negligent-hiring exposure that point-in-time vetting tools don't catch.
problem: Brokers get sued for negligent hiring/entrustment when a carrier they vetted months ago quietly lets its UCR registration, BOC-3 process-agent designation, or insurance lapse and then causes a loss — vetting at onboarding doesn't catch a mid-relationship lapse, which is exactly the ongoing-monitoring product category that firms like SaferWatch and CarrierOK sell as a distinct 'watchlist/monitoring' tier from their on-demand 'snapshot' search tier.
target_customer: Freight brokerages with an existing approved-carrier list (tens to low-hundreds of carriers) and factoring companies with a funded-carrier book, who need continuous rather than point-in-time compliance status.
evidence: The same incumbents that sell one-time carrier lookups also sell a separately-priced ongoing-monitoring product, proving the market treats 'watch this carrier over time' as distinct paid value: SaferWatch's own site distinguishes on-demand research from 'monitoring of your carrier watch list' within its $79.95/mo plan (fetched via search of https://truckbrokerinsurancenetwork.gtu-ins.com/why-we-and-you-should-use-saferwatch-for-carrier-selection/, 2026-08-19), and VerifyCarrier explicitly prices a separate 'Carrier Monitoring' product line ($49/$99/$249 per month for 50/250/unlimited monitored carriers with daily alerts on authority, insurance, and safety-rating changes) apart from its plain lookup API tiers (fetched https://verifycarrier.com/pricing, 2026-08-19). CarrierOK likewise runs a distinct no-contract monthly 'compliance' pricing page (https://www.carrier-ok.com/pricing?product=data, referenced via search 2026-08-19, page itself not yet directly fetched — flagged for confirmation before build).
knowledge_base: FMCSA Licensing & Insurance Socrata bulk datasets on data.transportation.gov — Active & Pending Insurance (qh9u-swkp) and Authority History (9mw4-x3tu), confirmed to exist via catalog.data.gov (fetched 2026-08-19) — for insurance-lapse and authority-status changes; the federal Unified Carrier Registration dataset on data.transportation.gov (fux9-ij6p), confirmed to exist via search of data.transportation.gov (fetched 2026-08-19, direct Socrata field/refresh-cadence confirmation still needed before build) for annual UCR compliance status; FMCSA QCMobile API for BOC-3/authority spot-checks between bulk refreshes (https://mobile.fmcsa.dot.gov/QCDevsite/docs/qcApi, fetched 2026-08-19). Staleness is detectable because Socrata datasets expose their own last-updated metadata and a failed/empty daily QCMobile spot-check flips a carrier to 'unconfirmed' rather than silently reporting old data.
autonomy_case: A1: broker self-signs-up, uploads their existing approved-carrier CSV (DOT numbers), pays via Stripe — no sales call needed, mirroring how VerifyCarrier's monitoring tiers are self-checkout. A2: the alert is a deterministic diff between yesterday's and today's pulled government field values (authority status, insurance-on-file flag, UCR-current flag) — no human reviews the diff. A3: if a data source is unreachable that day, the affected carriers are marked 'not reconfirmed since [date]' rather than silently showing stale green status, and the product never asserts a status it can't currently source. A4: nightly cron diff against the Socrata bulk files plus QCMobile spot-checks, with dataset vintage timestamps driving automatic staleness flags. A5: ingestion, diffing, and alert dispatch are all cron jobs with fail-closed behavior (no 'all clear' email if the day's pull failed). A6: zero per-customer human minutes — the product's entire job is turning a public-data diff into an email/webhook.
moat: None beyond focus and price — same public data as Idea 1 and the same incumbent set (SaferWatch, VerifyCarrier, CarrierOK) already sell this as a line item, so the wedge is bundling it as a cheap always-on companion to Idea 1's onboarding check rather than a separately-sold enterprise module, undercutting the $79.95-$249/mo price points found.
pricing_hypothesis: $39-$149/mo by number of monitored carriers (25/100/unlimited), positioned below SaferWatch's $79.95/mo all-in price and VerifyCarrier's $49-$249 monitoring tiers.
revenue_model: Recurring subscription tiered by watchlist size, self-serve Stripe billing.
time_to_first_revenue: 3-5 weeks: slightly longer than Idea 1 because it depends on reliably parsing the UCR and Authority History bulk files rather than only the keyless QCMobile ad-hoc endpoint, so initial build time is a bit higher.
risks: The UCR dataset's exact API/Socrata field structure and refresh schedule were found to exist but not yet fetched and field-verified — must confirm before committing to build. This idea overlaps substantially with Idea 1's data pipeline and target customer, so it is best pitched as a companion add-on tier of the same product rather than a fully separate company, and a founder choosing between the three should treat Ideas 1 and 3 as one product with two pricing tiers if resources are constrained.
why_simple: Every alert is a before/after diff on structured government fields (authority-active boolean, insurance-on-file boolean, UCR-current boolean) — there is no generative judgment call about whether a carrier is 'compliant,' only a direct read of what the public record currently says.
persona: Same builder profile as Idea 1 (freight-data-literate solo/small-team founder), packaging the ongoing-monitoring half of the same public-data pipeline as a distinct subscription tier for existing customers.

name: AssessGuard
one_liner: Portfolio-scale property-tax over-assessment monitor and flat-fee appeal-packet generator for landlords who own multiple rental parcels.
problem: Landlords with several rental properties get hit by annual assessment increases across multiple counties. Existing paid options are either contingency firms that take a cut of savings, or single-property flat-fee tools nobody has built for a whole portfolio with recurring, cycle-timed monitoring.
target_customer: SFR/small multifamily landlords and investor LLCs owning roughly 5-100 rental parcels, in one or more counties.
evidence: Ownwell runs a pure contingency model with 'no up-front costs... a contingency fee after we save you money,' percentage varies by region (ownwell.com/pricing, fetched 2026-08-19). TaxFightBack's own marketing characterizes Ownwell/TaxProper as taking '25%' of savings, calling contingency 'the most expensive option on successful appeals' (taxfightback.com/articles/competitor-comparisons/cheapest-way-to-appeal-property-taxes, fetched 2026-08-19). Flat-fee single-property alternatives already have real paying customers: AppealDesk sells a '$49 flat fee' evidence packet against a DIY baseline of '15-40 hours' of manual research (appealdesk.com/compare/appealdesk-vs-diy, fetched 2026-08-19); TaxFightBack sells its own packet for '$79' (same URL, fetched 2026-08-19). None of these serve a multi-parcel portfolio with recurring, cycle-timed monitoring.
knowledge_base: Cook County Assessor Open Data (Socrata): the Assessed Values dataset is live and machine-readable — GET https://datacatalog.cookcountyil.gov/resource/uzyt-m557.json returns JSON records with pin, year, class, township_code/name, nbhd, mailed/certified/board building-land-total values (fetched 2026-08-19, verified structure). Companion Parcel Sales dataset for comps: https://datacatalog.cookcountyil.gov/Property-Taxation/Assessor-Parcel-Sales/wvhk-k5uv (fetched 2026-08-19). Socrata datasets expose a rowsUpdatedAt metadata field usable on cron to detect staleness. Expansion counties (e.g. King County WA's assessor DataDownload portal, found via search 2026-08-19) still need live verification before being counted as covered — the King County page 503'd on direct fetch and is NOT yet confirmed.
autonomy_case: A1: self-serve signup, Stripe billing, portfolio parcel-ID upload, no sales call. A2: appeal packet is produced by a deterministic comp-selection function (same township/neighborhood code + property class, statistical median $/sqft) run against the open dataset, then rendered into a PDF template — no analyst touches it. A3: a parcel whose county has insufficient public comp data is explicitly excluded and unbilled ('insufficient public comp data for this parcel') rather than guessed at or routed to a human. A4: cron re-pulls each county's open dataset on its own refresh cadence and diffs the dataset's update metadata to detect staleness. A5: ingestion, packet generation, and Stripe dunning are all scheduled and fail-closed. A6: customer receives the packet and self-files (or self-e-files where offered) — no human touches an individual case, bounding support to FAQ-level.
moat: Per-county schema adapters across dozens of differently-shaped assessor open-data portals are real, compounding integration work; the recurring relationship is anchored to each county's annual assessment cycle.
pricing_hypothesis: $79-129 per parcel per assessment cycle standalone, or portfolio bundles ($299/mo up to 25 parcels, $599/mo up to 100) — materially cheaper than a 25%+ contingency fee once a portfolio has meaningful assessed value.
revenue_model: Annual/assessment-cycle subscription tiered by portfolio size, plus a one-time per-parcel packet fee for non-subscribers.
time_to_first_revenue: Fast — Cook County alone covers well over a million parcels with a verified live API; Stripe checkout can go live on day one for that county.
risks: Each county's assessor data has a different schema and refresh cadence, so coverage grows one county at a time (real engineering cost, not manual data curation, but still a scaling constraint); assessed-value data itself often only refreshes 1-3x/year, so 'freshness' claims must lean on the cron-diff staleness check rather than implying real-time data; comp selection must stay a deterministic, auditable statistic (never marketed as 'AI-selected' the way TaxFightBack markets its own product) to satisfy the AI-as-engine rule and avoid overpromising outcomes; must never promise a dollar savings figure, only present the computed gap.
why_simple: One cron job per county pulling a structured public dataset, one comp-selection function, one PDF template — no bespoke human work per customer.

name: SurplusSentry
one_liner: A nationwide, continuously-refreshed feed of county tax-sale excess-proceeds/surplus-funds postings with claim-deadline alerts, sold as a self-serve subscription to fund-recovery professionals and tax-deed investors.
problem: When a tax-deed or foreclosure sale nets more than what was owed, the county holds a surplus that the former owner (or lienholder) can claim — but there is no national list. Investors currently must go county-by-county: 'Contact the county clerk, treasurer, or tax collector... Many counties publish surplus fund lists on the office website; where it isn't posted, request it under your state's public-records law' (liensuite.com/tools/surplus-funds-guide, fetched 2026-08-19). Money already changes hands for exactly this data: LienSuite sells an 'Excess Proceeds standalone' subscription at '$49.99/mo' plus one-time per-county CSV snapshots at '$97' (liensuite.com/pricing, fetched 2026-08-19), while professional recovery agents earn fees the same guide describes as state-capped (e.g. 'Florida around 12% for assignees, California the greater of $2,500 or 5%,' 'Texas bar[s] non-attorneys from charging at all') (liensuite.com/tools/surplus-funds-guide, fetched 2026-08-19).
target_customer: Compliant fund-recovery agents, tax-deed/note investors, and title/escrow researchers who need to be first to a fresh surplus-funds posting across many counties.
evidence: See problem section: LienSuite's live pricing page confirms real, current paid demand for this exact data category at $49.99/mo and $97/county one-time (liensuite.com/pricing, fetched 2026-08-19).
knowledge_base: County treasurer/tax-collector 'excess proceeds'/'surplus funds' postings. Verified live example: LA County's Treasurer-Tax Collector publishes structured PDF lists per sale cycle (labeled '2026A,' '2025C,' etc.), searchable by item number or by Assessor's Identification Number, with instructions and claim forms alongside each list (ttc.lacounty.gov/notice-of-excess-proceeds, fetched 2026-08-19). Ingestion = deterministic PDF table extraction per county (fixed layout per jurisdiction), run on cron, diffed against the prior file hash/posting date to flag a new cycle or detect a county going stale past its expected posting window.
autonomy_case: A1: self-serve Stripe subscription, no sales call. A2: the deliverable — a structured, de-duplicated, cross-county surplus-funds list with a claim-deadline countdown — is produced entirely by the scrape+parse pipeline; nothing is drafted or filed on any individual's behalf. A3: any row the parser can't confidently extract is marked 'low confidence — verify against source PDF' with a direct link, rather than guessed at or routed to a human reviewer. A4: cron re-checks each county page/PDF and diffs file hash/last-modified to detect staleness. A5: ingestion, alerting, and billing are all scheduled and fail-closed. A6: the product never contacts a former owner or files a claim — it only supplies data to professional subscribers — so human minutes per customer are zero.
moat: Comprehensive, continuously-refreshed PDF-adapter coverage across hundreds of distinctly-formatted county pages is compounding integration work; being first to post a new list matters to this customer, so coverage breadth and latency are defensible.
pricing_hypothesis: $99-249/mo tiered by number of states/counties tracked, positioned above LienSuite's $49.99/mo single-purpose tier via broader county coverage and deadline-countdown alerting — still far below the value of a single professional recovery fee.
revenue_model: Tiered self-serve monthly SaaS subscription plus optional one-time full-history county exports.
time_to_first_revenue: Fast for jurisdictions with clean, verified PDF postings (confirmed live for LA County; LienSuite's own site claims existing coverage for Florida, Georgia, and Texas counties, per liensuite.com, fetched 2026-08-19) — expand county by county after.
risks: Source format is PDF, not a clean CSV/API, in most counties, so extraction is brittle to layout changes and needs ongoing (code-based, not manual-data) adapter maintenance; some states restrict who may be paid to help recover surplus funds, so marketing and product scope must stay strictly a data/alerts subscription and never drift into filing or contacting claimants on a customer's behalf; a live, lower-priced competitor (LienSuite) already exists in this exact niche, so differentiation must be real (coverage breadth, alert speed, deadline tracking) rather than repackaging.
why_simple: cron scrape to deterministic PDF table parse to dedupe/normalize to searchable DB to email/SMS alert — no bespoke human casework anywhere in the loop.

name: DocketRadius
one_liner: Address-radius rezoning, variance, and land-use hearing alerts for small property owners and local businesses, built on municipal legislative-tracking APIs instead of market-wide dashboards priced for CRE professionals.
problem: Cities publish zoning/variance/PUD hearing agendas through systems like Legistar, but knowing whether a hearing affects your specific address means manually watching every council/planning-commission agenda yourself. A paid product for the market-level version of this already exists and charges real money: ZoneWire sells 'New Meeting Alerts' for free and a Pro tier at '$39/month per market' with full transcripts, zoning analysis, and keyword alerts, self-serve with email-based signup and a 7-day trial, sourced from 'official public meeting records' of the relevant Commission/City Council bodies (zonewire.co/clark-county, fetched 2026-08-19) — but it is scoped and priced for an entire county market, not a single owner's block.
target_customer: Small landlords, HOA boards, and local small-business owners who want alerts only when a hearing could affect their specific parcel or block, not an entire market.
evidence: ZoneWire's live pricing page confirms real self-serve paid demand at $39/mo/market for this category (zonewire.co/clark-county, fetched 2026-08-19); a competitor named 'ReZone' surfaced in the same search offering dashboard/alert/API access to nationwide city-council land-use decisions, indicating more than one funded entrant already monetizing this docket-tracking niche.
knowledge_base: Legistar Web API — confirmed live and documented at webapi.legistar.com/Help (fetched 2026-08-19), exposing per-municipality-client endpoints: GET v1/{Client}/Matters, GET v1/{Client}/Matters/{MatterId}, GET v1/{Client}/Events, GET v1/{Client}/EventDates/{BodyId}, GET v1/{Client}/Events/{EventId}/EventItems. Legistar (Granicus) is used by hundreds of US city/county legislative bodies; matter records carry structured type/status/date fields suitable for deterministic keyword and status filtering rather than free-text interpretation.
autonomy_case: A1: self-serve address entry plus Stripe checkout, no sales call. A2: fulfilment is a cron poll of each subscribed municipality's Legistar API, a deterministic keyword match against zoning/variance/conditional-use/PUD matter types, and a geocode-and-radius match against the customer's saved address — the alert is generated from a template, not authored. A3: an address reference the geocoder can't confidently resolve is flagged 'unconfirmed — review source agenda item' with a direct link, rather than asserted as a match. A4: Legistar data is continuously updated by each municipality; staleness is detected per-client by checking each matter's LastModifiedUtc/EventDate fields on cron. A5: ingestion, geocoding, and alerting are all scheduled and fail-closed across many municipal clients. A6: zero human minutes per customer — support is bounded to onboarding/coverage FAQ.
moat: Knowing and maintaining which Legistar 'client' IDs exist, plus adapters for the non-Legistar systems (Granicus PrimeGov, CivicClerk) that other cities run, plus a working geocode/radius-matching layer, is compounding integration and data-modeling work.
pricing_hypothesis: $19-39/mo per tracked address; $99-299/mo portfolio tier for landlords/HOAs tracking many addresses across one or more cities — undercutting ZoneWire's $39/mo/market by scoping to an address instead of an entire market, viable at volume among low-touch subscribers.
revenue_model: Self-serve monthly SaaS subscription tiered by number of tracked addresses/municipalities.
time_to_first_revenue: Fast in any city already running Legistar — the API is live, documented, and requires no negotiation to start pulling data.
risks: Coverage is patchwork — not every city runs Legistar, so total addressable geography must be marketed honestly city-by-city; matching a legislative 'matter' to a precise parcel/radius is sometimes ambiguous when agenda text names a general area rather than an address, which must degrade to an 'unconfirmed match' per A3 rather than over-claim; the adjacent market-level tier already has at least two live/funded competitors (ZoneWire, ReZone), so the address-radius/consumer-landlord wedge must stay disciplined rather than drifting into competing head-on for CRE-analyst customers.
why_simple: cron poll of a documented public API, deterministic text and geo matching, template alert — no human review step anywhere.

name: PECOS Sentinel
one_liner: Automated Medicare revalidation & PECOS-deactivation deadline monitor for billing companies and group practices, built directly on CMS's own monthly revalidation feed.
problem: Every enrolled Medicare provider/supplier must revalidate on a CMS-set cycle (roughly every 3-5 years); MACs mail/portal notices 90-120 days out, and if the notice is missed the provider's billing privileges are deactivated with NO retroactive billing for the gap. Real practice reports: 'a revalidation notice had gone to a suite they left two years ago... they found out they were deactivated from a zero-dollar remittance, not a warning' and 'even a few weeks of lost billing can mean tens of thousands of dollars' (https://staffingly.com/insights/pain-points-solutions/medicare-deactivated-us-over-a-revalidation-notice-we-never-saw/, fetched via search 2026-08-19). Existing paid fixes are manual: credentialing firms charge ~$780 per individual revalidation (https://wchsb.com/services/credentialing-prices/) and $600-2,400/provider/year in ongoing credentialing maintenance (https://maverickhealthinnovations.com/blog/medical-credentialing-cost/), both fetched 2026-08-19.
target_customer: Medical billing / RCM companies and multi-provider group practices (5-200 NPIs) responsible for keeping their own or their clients' Medicare enrollment active.
evidence: Worse solutions already being paid for: (1) manual spreadsheet tracking, which fails as shown by the staffingly.com deactivation stories above; (2) credentialing consultancies charging $780/revalidation (WCH, fetched 2026-08-19) and $600-2,400/provider/year (Maverick Health, fetched 2026-08-19), most of which is opaque quote-based pricing rather than self-serve monitoring (https://qualigenix.com/medicare-revalidation-2026/, fetched 2026-08-19, notes most credentialing companies don't publish prices and sell via private quote).
knowledge_base: CMS 'Revalidation Due Date List' dataset, discoverable and machine-parseable via the official DCAT-US catalog at https://data.cms.gov/data.json (fetched 2026-08-19, 200 OK, 3MB JSON, 159 datasets). The dataset entry shows modified: 2026-08-05 and lists 40+ monthly CSV distributions back to 2022 (e.g. .../2026-08/1df6c395.../revalidation_base.csv, .../2026-07/..., .../2026-01/...). I directly fetched the live August-2026 file (HTTP 200, Last-Modified: Tue 04 Aug 2026) and confirmed columns: Enrollment ID, NPI, First/Last Name, Organization Name, Enrollment State Code, Provider Type Text, Enrollment Specialty, Revalidation Due Date, Adjusted Due Date, Individual Total Reassign To. Refresh cadence is monthly (verified by the run of dated directories from 2022-03 through 2026-08); staleness is self-detectable by diffing the data.json 'modified' field against an expected ~30-day cadence.
autonomy_case: A1: customer signs up, uploads/syncs their NPI roster, pays via Stripe, gets a dashboard/email/SMS — no sales call or manual provisioning. A2: fulfilment is a deterministic monthly join of the customer's NPI list against the freshly pulled CMS CSV; alerts are templated, not authored. A3: when an NPI's due date is 'TBD' (outside the 6-month CMS window) or absent from the file, the product says exactly that and shows the raw CMS row plus a direct PECOS link — it never guesses a date or advises on strategy. A4: cron pulls the CSV monthly from the URL data.json currently points to (not hardcoded), and flags itself stale if data.json's 'modified' timestamp hasn't advanced past 40 days. A5: ingestion, alert dispatch, and Stripe dunning are all cron/webhook driven, fail-closed (alerts if ingestion job fails). A6: support is bounded to 'here is what CMS's own list says about this NPI' — no case handling, no phone-tag with MACs.
moat: Archiving every monthly CMS snapshot since launch lets the product infer a provider's next due date even while CMS still shows 'TBD' (by pattern-matching each NPI's historical 3-5 year revalidation cadence) — a genuine data asset a same-day scraper of the current file can't replicate.
pricing_hypothesis: $79-249/mo tiered by NPIs monitored (25/100/500), undercutting the $780-per-event and $600-2,400/provider/year credentialing-firm alternative by an order of magnitude while running unattended.
revenue_model: Subscription SaaS, per-NPI-tier monthly billing via Stripe, annual discount.
time_to_first_revenue: 3-4 weeks: CSV ingestion + NPI matcher + alert templating + Stripe checkout is the whole build.
risks: CMS could rename the dataset or change its schema (mitigated by resolving the download URL from data.json each run instead of hardcoding it); customers must keep their own NPI roster current or the match silently misses new hires; the six-month lookahead window means 'TBD' NPIs need the historical-pattern moat to be genuinely useful, not just cosmetic.
why_simple: One join key (NPI), one date-threshold alerting engine, one monthly cron — no generative judgment anywhere in the fulfilment path.
persona: Healthcare public-data angle: provider-enrollment/PECOS compliance deadlines.

name: LabWatch CLIA
one_liner: Automated CLIA certificate expiration and status monitor for small clinics/labs and the billing companies that bill for them, sourced from CMS's own quarterly facility file — no manual date entry required.
problem: CLIA certificates (Waiver, PPM, Compliance, Accreditation) must be renewed on a fixed cycle, and a single overloaded office manager tracking it by hand is exactly the failure mode compliance vendors describe: renewal notices 'arrive in the mail alongside other regulatory correspondence' and get lost. When a certificate lapses, the consequence is immediate and mechanical, not judgment-based: 'if a claim is submitted to Medicare without a valid, active CLIA number, it will be denied at the front-end edit level, before a claims examiner ever reviews it' and penalties can run 'a few hundred dollars to thousands of dollars per day of non-compliance' with CMS able to stop all Medicare/Medicaid payments until compliance is proven (aggregated denial-code guidance, fetched via search 2026-08-19, e.g. https://www.mdclarity.com/denial-code-rarc/ma120, https://www.aapc.com/discuss/threads/clia-denials-qw.205236/).
target_customer: Small independent clinics/physician offices running waived or moderate-complexity testing, and the RCM/billing companies that process their lab claims.
evidence: A generic (manually-entered) expiration-tracking SaaS is already sold specifically against this pain: ExpirationReminder.com markets a dedicated 'CLIA Certification' tracking page (https://www.expirationreminder.com/document-tracking/clia-certification, fetched 2026-08-19) and its published pricing runs $49/mo (150 tracked items) up to $399/mo (2,500 items), all requiring the customer to manually key in every certificate's dates (https://www.expirationreminder.com/pricing, fetched 2026-08-19). That is money already changing hands for a strictly worse (manual-entry) version of what CMS's own public file can do automatically.
knowledge_base: CMS 'Provider of Services File - Clinical Laboratories' dataset, found in the same live data.json catalog (https://data.cms.gov/data.json, fetched 2026-08-19) with modified: 2026-07-16 and accrualPeriodicity 'R/P3M' (quarterly, machine-declared). I fetched the current Q2-2026 CSV directly (https://data.cms.gov/sites/default/files/2026-07/633ce84d.../Clia_DATA.Q2_2026.csv, HTTP 206 partial-content confirmed live) and verified the exact columns needed: CRTFCT_TYPE_CD (certificate type), CRTFCT_EFCTV_DT (effective date), TRMNTN_EXPRTN_DT (expiration date), CLIA_TRMNTN_CD (termination code), CMPLNC_STUS_CD (compliance status), plus facility name/address/CLIA number. Distribution history runs quarterly back to 2011, giving a verifiable refresh cadence for staleness detection.
autonomy_case: A1: self-serve signup, the clinic enters its own CLIA number(s) (or a billing company bulk-uploads its client roster), pays by card, no onboarding call. A2: fulfilment is a deterministic lookup/join against the freshly pulled quarterly file plus a date-threshold alert scheduler (180/90/30/7 days per the CMS renewal-bill cadence). A3: if a CLIA number isn't found in the latest file or its status code is ambiguous, the product states that plainly and links to the official QCOR lookup rather than inferring compliance status. A4: cron re-pulls the file each quarter (matching the declared R/P3M cadence) and cross-checks data.json's 'modified' field to detect a missed CMS refresh. A5: ingestion/alerts/billing all cron- and webhook-driven, fail-closed. A6: zero per-customer human minutes — the product only echoes what CMS's own record says.
moat: Bundling CLIA and Medicare-revalidation status (see PECOS Sentinel) into one per-NPI/per-facility compliance calendar is something neither the generic ExpirationReminder tool nor CMS's raw file offers on its own.
pricing_hypothesis: $39-149/mo by number of CLIA certificates tracked, priced below ExpirationReminder's $49-399/mo generic tiers while requiring zero manual data entry — a strictly better and cheaper offer.
revenue_model: Subscription SaaS, per-certificate tier, monthly or annual Stripe billing.
time_to_first_revenue: 3-4 weeks: same ingestion/alert skeleton as PECOS Sentinel, different dataset and join key (CLIA number).
risks: Quarterly (not monthly) refresh cadence means alert windows must be generous enough to survive a stale quarter; CLIA number formats/facility name matching can have edge cases; certificate fee schedules vary slightly by state agency even though the federal CMS file is the system of record for status.
why_simple: Same deterministic date-threshold engine as PECOS Sentinel, applied to a different but equally structured, quarterly-refreshed CMS file.
persona: Healthcare public-data angle: CLIA lab-certification compliance deadlines.

name: ExclusionAuto
one_liner: Flat-fee, unlimited-roster monthly OIG-LEIE + SAM.gov exclusion re-screening for small practices, home-health and staffing agencies, fully self-serve against the two federal machine-readable exclusion feeds.
problem: HHS-OIG requires providers to screen every employee and vendor against the federal exclusion lists, ideally monthly, because billing for services rendered even indirectly by an excluded individual creates civil monetary penalty exposure; small practices and staffing agencies with large hourly-worker rosters are the ones least equipped to do this by hand.
target_customer: Small physician practices, home-health/staffing agencies, and DME suppliers with rosters too large for manual monthly LEIE lookups but too small to negotiate an enterprise compliance contract.
evidence: A direct self-serve competitor already sells this: ExclusionScreening.com's published pricing shows Basic from $30/mo and Premium from $40/mo, with the Premium tier capped at 'up to 100 screens per month' covering OIG LEIE, GSA SAM, and the 46 state Medicaid exclusion lists, with 'custom pricing' gating anyone above that volume (https://exclusionscreening.com/pricing/, fetched via search 2026-08-19). That per-screen cap is exactly the gap a flat-fee, unlimited-roster automated re-screen can undercut for staffing agencies with turnover-heavy rosters of 200+ workers.
knowledge_base: Two federal, directly-fetched, machine-readable feeds: (1) HHS-OIG LEIE full database CSV at https://oig.hhs.gov/exclusions/downloadables/UPDATED.csv — fetched live 2026-08-19 (HTTP 200, 15.5MB), confirmed columns LASTNAME, FIRSTNAME, BUSNAME, NPI, EXCLTYPE, EXCLDATE, REINDATE, replaced monthly by OIG's own stated cadence ('updated by the 10th of every month', per https://oig.hhs.gov/exclusions/leie-database-supplement-downloads/); (2) GSA SAM.gov Exclusions Public Extract, a documented CSV/JSON API at https://api.sam.gov/entity-information/v4/download-exclusions (endpoint confirmed live/reachable, returns 404-without-key rather than DNS/connection failure, per GSA's own API docs at https://open.gsa.gov/api/exclusions-api/, fetched 2026-08-19), refreshed on a documented monthly-full/daily-incremental cadence per GSA's extract documentation.
autonomy_case: A1: self-serve signup, bulk roster upload (CSV or API), card payment, no sales call. A2: fulfilment is deterministic name/NPI matching against the freshly pulled LEIE and SAM CSVs, run on a schedule, producing a match/no-match report. A3: on an ambiguous name match (common surname collisions are LEIE's well-known weakness) the product flags it explicitly as 'needs manual confirmation - possible match, not certain' with the raw LEIE row shown, rather than asserting exclusion status — it degrades to showing evidence, never adjudicates. A4: LEIE re-pulled monthly per OIG's stated cadence, SAM re-pulled on GSA's documented extract schedule; staleness self-detected by comparing the file's declared update date to expected cadence. A5: ingestion, re-screening, and dunning all cron/webhook-driven, fail-closed. A6: no human review sits between roster upload and report — screening volume is unbounded by design (that's the differentiator vs. the incumbent's per-screen cap).
moat: Combining both federal feeds (many competitors emphasize LEIE alone) with unlimited, flat-fee re-screening removes the per-screen throttling that pushes larger rosters into the incumbent's opaque custom-quote tier — a structural pricing/product wedge, not just a cheaper clone.
pricing_hypothesis: $49/mo flat for unlimited roster size and unlimited monthly re-screens (vs. incumbent's $40/mo capped at 100 screens/mo), positioned specifically at staffing/home-health agencies whose rosters exceed that cap.
revenue_model: Subscription SaaS, flat monthly fee, Stripe billing, annual discount.
time_to_first_revenue: 2-3 weeks: this is the simplest of the three builds (two CSV feeds, one fuzzy-match engine, one report generator).
risks: This is the most competitively crowded of the three (ExclusionScreening.com, ProviderTrust, Verisys already operate here), so differentiation must hold on the uncapped-roster/self-serve-signup wedge rather than novelty of data access; name-matching false positives/negatives on a common-name file like LEIE are an inherent, disclosed limitation rather than a data-freshness problem.
why_simple: Pure deterministic string/ID matching against two well-documented federal CSV feeds — no generative or judgment component in the fulfilment path.
persona: Healthcare public-data angle: OIG/SAM exclusion screening for small practices and staffing agencies.

name: MaintFeeGuard
one_liner: Self-serve deadline alerts for US patent maintenance fees, computed deterministically from USPTO's free weekly bulk data — no annuity middleman markup, no human touches your payment.
problem: Patent owners forfeit patents by missing the 3.5/7.5/11.5-year maintenance fee windows; USPTO explicitly states it has no duty to remind patentees and treats missed payment as the patentee's sole responsibility, with recovery only via a formal 'unintentional delay' petition (fetched 2026-08-19: https://www.patenttrademarkblog.com/late-patent-maintenance-fee-payment/ and https://patentsunset.com/blog/what-happens-when-patent-maintenance-fees-go-unpaid, both describing lapse after the fee window plus 6-month grace surcharge period). A commercial market already exists to solve exactly this: PatentRenewal.com sells tiered plans ('Essential' for small portfolios up to 'Enterprise', plus per-renewal 'flat service fee', local agent fees, and a currency markup) explicitly to prevent missed renewals (fetched 2026-08-19: https://www.patentrenewal.com/pricing).
target_customer: Solo inventors and small patent holders / small IP-owning startups with 1-50 active US patents who don't want to pay a full-service annuity provider's per-renewal service fee and agent markups just to be told a date.
evidence: PatentRenewal.com's own pricing page (fetched 2026-08-19, https://www.patentrenewal.com/pricing) lists stacked cost categories — 'official IP renewal fees', a 'flat service fee per renewal', 'local agent fees', a 1-2% currency-exchange markup, and transaction fees — and offers a '30% savings guarantee' vs traditional renewal providers, proving buyers already pay recurring fees to avoid missing these deadlines. USPTO's own guidance (fetched 2026-08-19, https://www.patenttrademarkblog.com/late-patent-maintenance-fee-payment/) confirms the Office sends no mandatory reminder and that missing the window (with only a 6-month grace period at surcharge) causes irrevocable loss of enforceable rights absent a costly unintentional-delay petition — the pain that funds the existing paid category.
knowledge_base: USPTO Patent Maintenance Fee Events bulk file, dataset page https://data.uspto.gov/bulkdata/datasets/ptmnfee2 — confirmed live and reachable (HTTP 200 verified via curl, 2026-08-19). Per USPTO's own product description (surfaced via live web search of developer.uspto.gov, corroborated 2026-08-19): published weekly, every Tuesday at 3pm EST, at no charge, as a cumulative ASCII file (MaintFeeEvents_yyyymmdd.txt inside MaintFeeEvents.zip) containing patent number, application number, small/micro entity designation, filing date, grant/issue date, maintenance-fee event entry date, and event code — covering all patents granted since Sept 1, 1981. Because the fee windows (3.5/7.5/11.5 years post-grant, plus the 6-month grace period) are fixed by statute/CFR, the deadline for any patent is pure arithmetic on the grant date in this file; staleness is trivially detectable (expected file every Tuesday — a missed weekly drop is a hard signal).
autonomy_case: A1: signup + Stripe payment + enter patent numbers, no sales call, no onboarding. A2: a cron job diffs the weekly USPTO file, computes fee windows via a fixed formula, and emails/dashboards results — 100% code, no reviewer. A3: the product never advises on legal strategy or entity-size classification; it shows the official date/fee tier and links straight to USPTO's own fees.uspto.gov payment portal, degrading to 'confirm your entity size — we cannot determine this for you' rather than guessing or routing to a person. A4: corpus is the public weekly USPTO bulk file; a missing/late weekly drop is auto-detected against the known Tuesday cadence. A5: ingestion, digest emails, and Stripe dunning are all cron/webhook-driven. A6: no bespoke onboarding — customers self-add patent numbers; the product deliberately never touches or transmits customer payment to USPTO, eliminating the fiduciary/liability work that forces annuity firms into human account management.
moat: Cadence + breadth: rebuilding the full weekly-refreshed, statute-driven deadline engine across a customer's whole portfolio is a data-engineering chore competitors won't bother with for a low-ticket self-serve tier; underpricing full-service annuity firms (who carry agent networks and FX handling) by never touching money is a structural cost advantage they can't match without gutting their own business model.
pricing_hypothesis: $9-29/mo flat for up to 25 tracked patents (undercutting PatentRenewal's stacked service-fee-per-renewal + agent-fee model), $79-149/mo for larger portfolios (50-250 patents) aimed at small firms/solo patent agents managing several inventors' portfolios.
revenue_model: Flat-tier monthly SaaS subscription by number of tracked patents, self-serve Stripe billing, annual plan discount.
time_to_first_revenue: 2-3 weeks: ingest one weekly bulk file, build the fixed-window deadline calculator, ship a minimal upload/CSV + email-alert MVP, launch self-serve checkout.
risks: Not yet verified: actual USPTO fee amounts per entity size and the exact CFR citation for the 3.5/7.5/11.5-year windows (must pull from the authoritative MPEP/CFR text before launch, not memory). Small/micro entity status isn't in the bulk file for all periods and must be self-reported by the customer, which is a manual data point (though it degrades safely per A3). Conversion risk: patent holders may just rely on their prosecuting attorney's existing docketing system for free.
why_simple: One weekly public flat file, one fixed statutory formula, one cron job, one email — no NLP, no scraping, no legal judgment calls, nothing to keep an eye on except 'did this week's file arrive.'

name: MarkDocket
one_liner: Flat-rate, self-serve trademark deadline docketing (Office Action responses, Statement of Use, Section 8/9/71 windows) built directly on USPTO's live TSDR API, priced for solo filers and small brands shut out of $60+/mo law-firm docketing platforms.
problem: Trademark owners lose registrations or applications to missed statutory deadlines (Office Action response, Statement of Use, post-registration Section 8/9 maintenance) because there is no free official reminder system comparable to what law firms buy. The market rate for this exact function is already established and non-trivial: Alt Legal's IP docketing software prices strictly by number of docketed matters, from $60/month for up to 50 matters to $295/month for up to 400 matters (fetched 2026-08-19: https://www.altlegal.com/pricing/) — pricing squarely aimed at firms, not the solo filer or small brand with 1-10 marks.
target_customer: Solo trademark applicants, small business owners, and boutique/one-attorney firms with a handful of live marks who need deadline tracking but are priced out of, or overserved by, full law-firm docketing suites.
evidence: Alt Legal's own pricing page (fetched 2026-08-19, https://www.altlegal.com/pricing/) confirms recurring monthly fees of $60-$295 scaled by matter count for exactly this docketing function, plus a paid '+$30 to +$95/mo' add-on tier specifically for trademark watch/match features — clear proof of an established willingness to pay for automated deadline and monitoring service in this category, at a price point far above what a 1-10-mark owner needs or can justify.
knowledge_base: USPTO TSDR (Trademark Status & Document Retrieval) API. Live-verified 2026-08-19: a direct request to https://tsdrapi.uspto.gov/ts/cd/casestatus/sn88888888/info.json returned HTTP 401 (Unauthorized) — confirming the endpoint is live and gated behind a free registered API key, exactly as documented. USPTO's own bulk-data page (fetched 2026-08-19: https://www.uspto.gov/trademarks/apply/check-status-view-documents/trademark-bulk-data) confirms free API-key registration and a companion Bulk Data Storage System. Status responses (JSON/XML) expose prosecution history including document mailing dates, from which statutory deadlines (Office Action response window, Statement of Use 6-month window from Notice of Allowance, Section 8/71 5-6yr and 9-10yr renewal windows) are computed by fixed rule, not judgment. Staleness is self-detecting: any serial number whose TSDR record hasn't updated on the expected polling cadence flags itself.
autonomy_case: A1: sign up, pay by card, paste in serial/registration numbers — no onboarding call. A2: a scheduled job polls TSDR per tracked mark, applies fixed statutory-deadline rules to the returned prosecution-history dates, and pushes calendar/email alerts — all code, zero manual docketing. A3: when TSDR data is ambiguous (e.g., an unusual office action type the rule table doesn't cover), the product flags 'unrecognized event — verify manually via TSDR' rather than guessing or routing to a person; it never gives legal advice on how to respond. A4: TSDR is the live USPTO system of record, refreshed continuously by USPTO itself; the product's own poll cadence (e.g., daily) is trivially monitored for failures. A5: polling, alerting, and billing dunning are all cron/webhook-based. A6: no bespoke per-customer setup beyond entering case numbers; support load is bounded because the product only ever states official USPTO dates, never interprets them.
moat: Price-tier wedge under an established category: Alt Legal has already proven and priced the demand, but its per-matter pricing structurally can't go low enough for a 1-10-mark solo owner without cannibalizing its firm business — a flat cheap tier serving that segment doesn't compete head-on, it captures underserved demand the incumbent's own pricing page shows it's not built for.
pricing_hypothesis: $15-19/mo flat for up to 10 tracked marks (vs. Alt Legal's $60/mo floor for up to 50 matters), $39-59/mo for up to 50 marks aimed at solo practitioners.
revenue_model: Flat monthly SaaS subscription tiered by number of tracked marks, self-serve billing, no per-seat law-firm pricing complexity.
time_to_first_revenue: 3-4 weeks: register a TSDR API key, build the fixed deadline-rule engine against prosecution-history events, ship serial-number entry + email-alert MVP.
risks: TSDR API rate limits (reported in live search as 60 req/min/key for status, 4 req/min/key for document downloads — not independently re-verified against a rate-limit response in this session) could constrain portfolio size per key at scale. The exact current statutory response windows (e.g., 3-month vs 6-month Office Action response period under USPTO's 2022/2023 rule changes) must be pulled from the authoritative CFR/TMEP text before launch, not assumed. Some deadline types (e.g., extension-of-time filings) add branching logic that must be modeled carefully to avoid a wrong date ever being shown.
why_simple: One authenticated public API per mark, one fixed rule table mapping USPTO event codes to statutory deadlines, one polling cron, one alert email — no generative judgment anywhere in the deadline calculation.

name: MarkCollide
one_liner: Daily automated trademark-collision watch scored by deterministic name-similarity + Nice-class overlap against USPTO's free daily filing feed, undercutting Markify's per-mark annual watch pricing.
problem: Brand owners must catch confusingly similar marks filed by others quickly (to oppose during the 30-day publication window) or lose the cheap opposition option and face costlier cancellation/litigation later. A paid market for exactly this monitoring already exists and is priced per mark per year.
target_customer: Solo brand owners, DTC/Amazon sellers, and small businesses with 1-20 registered or pending marks who currently either pay per-mark watch fees or do nothing and rely on luck.
evidence: Markify's trademark watch service page (fetched directly 2026-08-19: https://www.markify.com/services/trademark-watch.html) lists live prices — US Federal Full watch at $39/year, EU Full at $59/year, Global (190 registers) at $129/year, with 'single registers from $39/year' — confirming an established, itemized willingness to pay specifically for ongoing new-filing collision monitoring, at a price a single-mark small owner is already paying today.
knowledge_base: USPTO Trademark Daily XML File (TDXF) — Applications dataset. Live-verified 2026-08-19: the dataset landing page https://data.uspto.gov/bulkdata/datasets/TRTDXFAP returned HTTP 200 (confirmed via curl), and the raw daily files are also published at https://bulkdata.uspto.gov/data/trademark/dailyxml/applications/ per USPTO's own developer.uspto.gov product listing (surfaced via live search 2026-08-19, title: 'Trademark daily XML file (TDXF) applications | ... Open Data Portal'). Per that USPTO product description, the free daily XML files (per the U.S. Trademark Assignments/Applications DTD) contain word mark, serial number, filing date, goods & services text, international classification number(s), status code(s), and design search codes for every newly filed application — refreshed daily, so staleness (a missing day's file) is immediately detectable against the known daily cadence.
autonomy_case: A1: self-serve signup, enter your mark(s) + classes, pay by card — no analyst call, unlike a watch-service 'report' delivered by a human search analyst at some competitors. A2: a daily cron job parses the new day's XML feed and runs a deterministic string-similarity (edit distance/phonetic) + Nice-class-overlap scoring function against the customer's marks, emitting a ranked hit list — pure code, no analyst review queue. A3: the product never opines on likelihood of confusion or advises opposing; it shows the raw new filing, its computed similarity score, and a link to the official TSDR record, explicitly narrowing to 'potential textual/class overlap — you decide whether to consult counsel,' degrading gracefully rather than escalating. A4: the daily USPTO XML feed is public and machine-readable; a missed day's file is a detectable gap against the known daily publish cadence. A5: daily ingestion, scoring, alert emails, and billing dunning are all schedulable/cron-driven. A6: zero human minutes per customer — matching runs identically across all customers' watched marks with no bespoke set-up beyond entering a wordmark and class list.
moat: Freshness + price: daily ingestion (vs. Markify's report-cycle model) plus a much lower per-mark price is achievable specifically because there's no human analyst in the loop — a structural cost advantage over the human-reviewed 'ranked, exportable report' model Markify itself advertises, not just a feature checklist difference.
pricing_hypothesis: $9-15/mo per watched mark (US federal only) undercutting Markify's $39/yr per-register price when annualized against a small owner's real usage, $29-49/mo for a 5-mark small-portfolio bundle.
revenue_model: Per-mark or portfolio-tier monthly SaaS subscription, self-serve billing, upsell to multi-jurisdiction watch as a later add-on once state/foreign feeds are integrated.
time_to_first_revenue: 3-4 weeks: parse the daily XML feed, build the similarity + class-overlap scoring engine, ship mark-entry + daily-digest email MVP.
risks: Similarity scoring needs careful tuning (naive edit-distance alone produces too many false positives/negatives for real trademark 'confusing similarity' analysis) — must be validated against known TTAB opposition fact patterns before claiming accuracy, and must be marketed strictly as a monitoring/screening tool, not legal advice, to stay clear of the AI-as-engine and A3 boundaries. Design-mark/logo collisions (image similarity) are out of scope for a text/XML-only v1, which narrows the addressable pain vs. full-service competitors that also watch figurative marks.
why_simple: One public daily XML feed, one deterministic string+class matching function, one digest email — the algorithm ranks and presents, it never renders a legal opinion.

name: WARN Signal
one_liner: Automated, code-fulfilled layoff-notice intelligence feed (alerts, search, API, CSV export) built from state WARN Act filings, refreshed on cron instead of by hand.
problem: Every mass layoff/plant closing over the WARN Act threshold must be filed with a state workforce agency, but the 50 states publish these filings in 50 different formats (some true APIs, some XLSX, some PDF-only), so buyers who need fast, structured layoff signal today either scrape it themselves or pay a vendor whose 'live' product still has a human step in the loop. WARNTracker's own pricing page states its top-tier 'Live Airtable view' spreadsheet is 'accessible within 1 business day' of purchase — i.e. a person provisions it — at $250 upfront plus $250/month, or $2,000 one-time for the historical CSV (fetched https://www.warntracker.com/pricing, 2026-08-19). That is the 'worse, human-touched, expensive' incumbent this product undercuts with a purely automated pipeline.
target_customer: Staffing/recruiting agencies, corporate outplacement and career-transition firms, commercial real-estate/office-liquidation brokers, and distressed-asset or PE sourcing teams who want to know about a mass layoff within hours of the state filing, not after a newsletter roundup.
