evidence: WARNTracker charges $250/mo (+$250 upfront) or a $2,000 one-time historical CSV for WARN data, and its premium tier is explicitly delivered with a 1-business-day human turnaround (fetched https://www.warntracker.com/pricing, 2026-08-19) — proving both that money already changes hands for this data and that the current 'live' offering isn't actually code-only. A free competitor (layoffdata.com) also exists per search results, confirming there's enough demand to support multiple players at different price/quality points.
knowledge_base: Texas publishes its WARN notices as a true public Socrata JSON API — verified live by fetching https://data.texas.gov/resource/8w53-c4f6.json?$order=notice_date+DESC&$limit=5 on 2026-08-19, which returned HTTP 200 with records through notice_date 2026-06-23 (JPMorgan Chase, Plano TX, 244 workers) — proving the feed is current to within ~8 weeks of today. California's EDD publishes its statewide WARN report as a structured XLSX at a stable URL — verified live via `curl -o /dev/null` on https://edd.ca.gov/siteassets/files/jobs_and_training/warn/warn_report1.xlsx on 2026-08-19, returning HTTP 200, a valid spreadsheet content-type, and 44,918 bytes. Staleness is detectable per-state by diffing max(notice_date) against the cron run date; a state whose feed hasn't advanced past its historical cadence is flagged low-confidence rather than silently shown as current. Other states (NY, WA, MA) run their own WARN dashboards per search results and would need per-state verification during build (some may only offer PDF/manual-request data, which the product would exclude or clearly mark as unsupported/degraded coverage rather than fabricate).
autonomy_case: A1: Stripe self-serve signup issues dashboard/API access instantly, no demo or provisioning call. A2: fulfilment is a cron ETL (pull each state's API/file, normalize schema, dedupe, push to a searchable store, fire webhook/email alerts) — entirely code, no review queue. A3: when a state source is unreachable or its data hasn't moved past its expected cadence, that state is shown as 'stale as of <date>' with the raw source link rather than guessed at, and the product's scope is explicitly 'here are the filings,' not legal/compliance advice, so there's no ambiguous case requiring a human judgment call. A4: nightly/weekly cron re-pulls per-state sources; staleness is a computed field (max filing date vs. run date), not manually tracked. A5: ingestion, alert delivery and Stripe dunning are all cron/webhook driven and fail closed (a broken state feed stops publishing new alerts for that state instead of guessing). A6: support load is bounded because the product's only promise is 'structured, timestamped copies of public filings' — there is no bespoke research or case handling to escalate.
moat: The underlying filings are public, so the moat isn't data exclusivity — it's the unglamorous integration work of normalizing ~50 non-uniform state formats (API vs. XLSX vs. scrape-resistant PDF) into one clean schema with per-source freshness tracking, kept current as states change their publishing formats, priced and delivered faster than the $250+/mo human-touched incumbent.
pricing_hypothesis: $79-$149/mo for real-time multi-state alerts + search (undercutting WARNTracker's $250/mo), with a $249-$399 one-time full-history export as the anchor-priced upsell (vs. WARNTracker's $2,000) — pricing power comes from having zero manual fulfillment cost, not from being cheaper on data itself.
revenue_model: Tiered monthly SaaS subscription (state coverage / alert volume / API access gated by tier) plus a one-time historical-export upsell, billed and dunned entirely through Stripe.
time_to_first_revenue: Days to a few weeks: an MVP covering the ~10-15 highest-filing-volume states with confirmed structured sources (Texas API and California XLSX already verified live) can launch self-serve billing immediately; broader state coverage is additive, not a launch blocker.
risks: State-by-state format fragility is the core engineering risk — only Texas and California were verified live in this session; several other states may publish WARN data only as PDFs or on-request email lists, which would need to be excluded or clearly flagged as unsupported rather than silently missing from alerts. The space already has a free player (layoffdata.com) and a paid incumbent (WARNTracker), so differentiation has to be real-time automation and API access, not just existence. Filing volume is inherently lumpy (macro-dependent), which affects revenue predictability more than product risk.
why_simple: No AI judgment is required anywhere in the pipeline — every field (company, location, headcount, dates) is copied verbatim from a structured government filing, normalized by deterministic code, and delivered by webhook/API/export; there is no generative step in the path from public filing to customer-visible number.
persona: Workforce & immigration public data angle — DOL/state WARN Act layoff-notice disclosures as B2B sales/market intelligence.

name: SponsorScope
one_liner: A searchable, always-refreshed database of which U.S. employers actually filed H-1B/PERM sponsorship paperwork, at what wage, and how often — built entirely from DOL's own quarterly disclosure files — sold to recruiters and staffing agencies who need to know before they submit a candidate.
problem: Tech and healthcare recruiters routinely waste submittals pitching candidates who need visa sponsorship to employers that, per the public record, rarely or never file H-1B/PERM paperwork, or that file at wage levels far below what the recruiter is quoting. The government publishes the ground truth (every LCA and PERM filing, with employer, job title, wage and status) but only as raw quarterly spreadsheets with tens of millions of rows spanning 15+ years, not as a searchable product — which is exactly the gap that already-monetized third-party tools (a $199 'Sponsorship Premium' product on Gumroad, and free-to-freemium sites like MyVisaJobs and H1BGrader per search results) are built to fill.
target_customer: Tech/healthcare recruiting and staffing agencies, and RPO (recruitment process outsourcing) teams, who need employer-level sponsorship-history and wage-benchmark lookups before spending time on a submittal — priced as a per-seat or per-search SaaS tool, not a compliance product.
evidence: A live Gumroad product titled 'Sponsorship Premium' sells access to H-1B sponsorship data for $199 (confirmed by fetching https://maurobonfietti.gumroad.com/l/sponsor-premium on 2026-08-19, where the page's embedded pricing metadata reads `"price":199.0,"priceCurrency":"USD"`), demonstrating real money already changes hands for exactly this kind of employer-sponsorship lookup built on the same public LCA data. Search results independently surfaced MyVisaJobs and H1BGrader as established players in this same 'H-1B sponsor database' niche, indicating a durable market rather than a one-off product.
knowledge_base: DOL's Office of Foreign Labor Certification (OFLC) Performance Data page publishes the full LCA (H-1B/H-1B1/E-3) and PERM disclosure files every fiscal quarter as structured Excel workbooks with documented record layouts, with history back to FY2008. Verified live on 2026-08-19: `curl` against https://www.dol.gov/media/LCA_Disclosure_Data_FY2026_Q3.xlsx returned HTTP 200, content-type `application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.spreadsheetml.sheet`, 251,850,891 bytes; the equivalent PERM file at https://www.dol.gov/media/PERM_Disclosure_Data_FY2026_Q3.xlsx returned HTTP 200, same content-type, 156,267,808 bytes. The OFLC performance index page (fetched https://www.dol.gov/agencies/eta/foreign-labor/performance, 2026-08-19) confirms this is a standing quarterly release with a documented record-layout PDF per file, so staleness is detectable by checking for the next fiscal-quarter file appearing on a fixed post-quarter-end schedule.
autonomy_case: A1: self-serve account creation and Stripe checkout give immediate search/API access, no sales call. A2: fulfilment is a quarterly batch ETL (download the new disclosure file, normalize employer names/NAICS/wage fields, load into a search index) plus a deterministic query engine for the customer-facing lookups — no analyst reviews or edits a result before it's shown. A3: employer-name matching across years is fuzzy by nature (mergers, staffing-agency vs. end-client naming); rather than guessing, the product shows all plausible matches with a confidence indicator and the raw filing IDs so the user can disambiguate themselves, and returns 'no filings found in the public record' when there's genuinely no match instead of speculating. A4: a cron job checks for each program's next-quarter file on DOL's site on a schedule keyed to DOL's own quarterly release cadence, and the UI displays 'data current through FY2026 Q3, filed by DOL' so staleness is visible, not hidden. A5: ETL, indexing and billing are all schedulable and idempotent (safe to re-run), and fail closed by keeping serving the last-good quarter if a new file's schema doesn't validate. A6: the product's job is bounded to 'search public filings by employer/title/wage,' with no bespoke research, so support volume doesn't scale with customer count.
moat: The raw data is public and already has free/cheap competitors, so the moat is (a) 15+ years of schema-drifted quarterly files cleaned into one consistent, fast-searchable index, (b) employer-name deduplication/fuzzy-matching that raw spreadsheet users have to redo themselves every time, and (c) packaging and pricing specifically for the recruiter/staffing workflow (per-search or per-seat, integrable into an ATS) rather than the general-public lookup UX competitors ship today.
pricing_hypothesis: $49-$149/mo per-seat for recruiter/staffing-agency search access (below the $199 one-time Gumroad anchor but recurring, reflecting continuous refresh value), with a metered API tier for ATS/CRM integrations priced per 1,000 lookups.
revenue_model: Monthly per-seat SaaS subscription plus a metered API add-on, billed via Stripe; no historical one-time sale needed since the value is the always-refreshed lookup, not a static export.
time_to_first_revenue: Two to four weeks: the current-quarter file is already confirmed downloadable today, so the main lift before launch is the initial ETL/index build over the historical quarterly archive (a one-time batch job, not an ongoing dependency) plus the search UI.
risks: DOL's file schema and column names have drifted across fiscal years/quarters historically (visible in the range of filenames from FY2008 onward), so the ETL needs to tolerate schema changes without silently mis-mapping fields. The ~1-quarter publication lag means the product cannot claim 'real-time' sponsorship status, only 'most recent published filings' — must be stated clearly to avoid overpromising. The niche must stay strictly framed as 'historical sponsorship record + disclosed wage benchmarking' and never drift into computing or asserting a required prevailing-wage rate, which would cross into excluded territory. Free/cheap incumbents (MyVisaJobs, H1BGrader, the $199 Gumroad product) mean differentiation has to be real (recruiter workflow, API, seat pricing), not just 'we also have the data.'
why_simple: Every number shown (employer name, job title, filed wage, case status, filing count) is copied directly from DOL's own disclosure spreadsheet by deterministic ETL code; the only place any matching logic is applied is employer-name disambiguation, which is surfaced to the user as multiple ranked candidates rather than a single asserted answer, so no generative or judgment-based step ever produces the number a customer relies on.
persona: Workforce & immigration public data angle — DOL LCA/PERM disclosure files as B2B sponsorship-history and salary-benchmarking intelligence for recruiters/staffing agencies.

name: QueueGuard
one_liner: Automated deadline and status-change monitoring for solar/storage/wind interconnection queue positions across ISO/RTO public queue files, so developers never get bounced from a queue for missing a milestone.
problem: Developers with projects scattered across CAISO, ERCOT, PJM, MISO, SPP, NYISO and ISO-NE must track dozens of queue positions, each governed by strict milestone-payment, financial-security and interconnection-agreement deadlines set inside these tariffs. Missing one triggers automatic withdrawal and loss of queue position, forcing a full re-application at the back of the line and breaking ITC safe-harbor timing and SREC eligibility. Today this is tracked by manually re-downloading and diffing monthly/weekly ISO spreadsheets in Excel.
target_customer: Small-to-mid independent solar/storage/wind developers and IPPs (roughly 5-150 employees) with 10-100 active interconnection requests across two or more ISOs, plus interconnection consultants managing client portfolios.
evidence: Missed-deadline consequences (queue withdrawal, full requeue, broken ITC safe harbor) are documented: 'missing a deadline on PG&E interconnection applications can mean PTO revocation, queue position loss, or full resubmission' (https://www.pandwsolar.com/sce-pto-delays-solar-storage-interconnection-guide/, fetched 2026-08-19) and 'When you miss your window for interconnection... you fall back by a full cycle... a missed ITC safe harbor window, a broken SREC registration, or a customer who simply walks away' (https://energyscaperenewables.com/post/solar-interconnection-critical-path-2026/, fetched 2026-08-19). Money already changes hands for packaged versions of this exact queue data: GridTracker's Interconnection.fyi states 'The complete dataset — including developer names, documents, and daily updates — is available through GridTracker, with monthly CSV delivery and daily Snowflake direct-share subscription options' (https://www.interconnection.fyi/, fetched 2026-08-19).
knowledge_base: CAISO Public Queue Report — https://www.caiso.com/documents/publicqueuereport.xlsx — confirmed live by direct fetch 2026-08-19: resolves to a real 376KB .xlsx (OOXML/ZIP signature verified), no login. ERCOT GIS Report — https://www.ercot.com/mp/data-products/data-product-details?id=PG7-200-ER — confirmed live by direct fetch 2026-08-19: metadata page states format 'xlsx', availability 'Public, EWS' (Extract Web Service, i.e. API-accessible), generation frequency 'Chron - Monthly', no login required, most recent metadata update Feb 9 2026. Additional ISOs (PJM, MISO, SPP, NYISO, ISO-NE) are documented in search results as publishing structurally similar public queue spreadsheets, but PJM's own domain returned HTTP 403/503 to automated fetch this session (bot-blocked — not confirmed live by me, needs a registered API path in build phase). Staleness is detectable via each file's own embedded snapshot/report date.
autonomy_case: A1: card signup, no account connections needed (source data is public), automated email/SMS alerts, self-serve cancel. A2: cron job downloads each ISO's file, diffs against the last snapshot, computes deadlines from the file's own milestone-schedule columns — no review queue. A3: when a customer's queue number can't be matched in a given ISO's file the product flags 'unmatched — confirm queue number' rather than inferring a deadline; every deadline shown cites the exact file and snapshot date it came from. A4: scheduled re-download of public xlsx files with embedded snapshot dates giving automatic staleness detection. A5: a batch ingestion/alerting pipeline that is fully cron-schedulable and fails closed (sends an 'ingestion failed / data may be stale' warning rather than silently serving old dates). A6: onboarding is self-service (customer enters/searches their own queue numbers); no bespoke per-customer integration since each ISO's file schema is standardized across all its filers.
moat: Each ISO runs its own distinct tariff-defined milestone rulebook — building and maintaining correct deadline logic per ISO is fiddly, unglamorous domain work. A developer's whole portfolio mapped into the tool creates real switching cost, and an accumulating historical snapshot archive (queue-delay patterns per ISO) becomes a data asset new entrants can't replicate without years of collected history.
pricing_hypothesis: $99-$399/mo tiered by number of tracked queue positions, undercutting bespoke consultant tracking and roughly in line with what GridTracker already charges for comparable packaged queue data access.
revenue_model: Monthly self-serve SaaS subscription, card billing, auto-renew, tiered by tracked-project count.
time_to_first_revenue: 4-6 weeks: MVP launches on CAISO + ERCOT (both independently confirmed as clean live public xlsx downloads), expanding to PJM/MISO/SPP/NYISO/ISO-NE once each ISO's access path (API key or scrape-resistant fetch) is confirmed.
risks: PJM (and possibly other ISOs) use bot protection that blocked generic automated fetch this session — may require registered API credentials or headless-browser fetching, adding build lift; queue file schemas change over time and need ongoing maintenance; ERCOT's file updates only monthly, capping alert lead-time granularity for that ISO; value depends on customers supplying accurate queue-ID mappings at onboarding.
why_simple: Two ISOs (CAISO, ERCOT) are already independently verified as clean, structured, publicly downloadable spreadsheets with a project ID as the natural join key — the MVP is a diff-and-alert job on data that already exists in the right shape.

name: DMR Sentinel
one_liner: Weekly monitoring of a facility's own NPDES Discharge Monitoring Report filings and permit limits against EPA's national ICIS-NPDES data, flagging missed DMR deadlines and effluent-limit exceedances before they escalate into EPA's Significant Noncompliance record.
problem: EPA's own compliance documentation states that failure to submit a timely, accurate DMR is treated as a formal 'significant violation,' and that DMR values not received within 31 days of the due date generate a violation code — with permittee failure to report timely, accurate and complete DMRs described as 'the single largest source of SNC nationwide.' Small-to-mid direct dischargers without dedicated compliance software track permit limits and lab results in spreadsheets and typically only discover a miss when EPA already shows it on the public ECHO record.
target_customer: EHS/environmental compliance managers at small-to-mid industrial dischargers and small municipal WWTPs with direct NPDES permits and 1-5 outfalls, who have no budget for enterprise EHS suites like Locus or Intelex.
evidence: EPA states DMR values not received within 31 days generate a formal violation code, and that DMR non-reporting/faulty reporting is the single largest source of Significant Noncompliance nationwide (search summary of https://usepa.servicenowservices.com and https://echo.epa.gov DMR guidance material, fetched 2026-08-19). A directly comparable paid product category already exists at real prices: NPDESPro (adjacent stormwater/NPDES compliance software) lists 'Starting Price $3500 Flat Rate, Per Year' on its Capterra listing (https://www.capterra.com/p/162369/NPDESPro/, fetched 2026-08-19) — roughly $292/mo for a broader enterprise tool than the narrow permit-holder monitor proposed here.
knowledge_base: EPA ECHO ICIS-NPDES DMR bulk downloads, confirmed by direct fetch of https://echo.epa.gov/tools/data-downloads (2026-08-19), which lists live file URLs including https://echo.epa.gov/files/echodownloads/npdes_dmrs_fy2026.zip (~100MB) plus prior fiscal years back before 2009, with the page's own stated refresh policy: 'All other DMR datasets are refreshed weekly' (only pre-FY2010 files are monthly). The companion ICIS-NPDES Permit Limit dataset on the same page supplies each facility's numeric permit limits to compare filed DMR values against. Staleness is detectable via the weekly file's fiscal-year coverage versus current date.
autonomy_case: A1: self-serve signup, customer enters their own NPDES permit ID(s), pays by card, receives automated alerts, cancels anytime — no sales call. A2: a cron job pulls the weekly ICIS-NPDES zip, filters to the customer's permit ID(s), and deterministically compares filed/missing DMR rows and reported values against the permit-limit dataset — a pure data comparison, no human review queue. A3: when a permit ID isn't yet visible in a given week's file (EPA notes states get up to a 40-day window to share DMR data with EPA), the product states exactly that — 'not yet visible in EPA's national system as of [date], typically posts within 40 days of state submission' — rather than asserting a compliance status it can't source. A4: EPA's own weekly-refresh cadence with a documented file-date used for cron scheduling and staleness flags. A5: fully scriptable weekly batch ingest that fails closed (alerts the operator if a download fails or row counts look anomalous) instead of silently serving stale data. A6: zero human minutes per customer beyond a one-time permit-ID entry; no bespoke integration required since ICIS-NPDES is a single nationally standardized schema.
moat: Correctly matching permit IDs to facilities and normalizing parameter codes/units across states' varying DMR conventions is deep, unglamorous domain work most teams underprice doing right. A customer's multi-year DMR history accumulating inside the tool as the system of record for their compliance calendar creates real switching cost.
pricing_hypothesis: $79-$249/mo per facility, well under NPDESPro's ~$292/mo enterprise-tier baseline for a narrower, permit-holder-specific alerting tool, with a per-outfall add-on for larger facilities.
revenue_model: Monthly per-facility self-serve SaaS subscription, card billing, tiered by outfall count.
time_to_first_revenue: 4-6 weeks — ICIS-NPDES DMR and permit-limit datasets are already confirmed live and directly downloadable; the core build is the ingestion/matching/comparison pipeline, not data acquisition.
risks: EPA's up-to-40-day state-to-EPA data-sharing lag means some very recent misses won't yet appear in the federal file (mitigated by A3-style self-disclosure of data lag); parameter-code and limit-unit normalization across states is genuinely messy and needs careful QA before alerts can be trusted; the addressable self-serve-priced segment (small permit holders not already on Locus/Intelex) needs demand validation beyond the comparable-pricing evidence found here.
why_simple: The federal weekly zip files use permit ID as a clean join key — a single facility's own record is a small, deterministic filter-and-diff job against data already confirmed to exist in machine-readable form, with no scraping of heterogeneous state portals required.

name: SDWIS Compliance Clock
one_liner: Pairs EPA's national drinking-water violation database with a coded regulatory-deadline calendar so small water systems know exactly when their next Consumer Confidence Report, monitoring test, or public-notification deadline falls, before their state has to tell them.
problem: Small community water systems typically run without dedicated compliance staff, yet must hit deadlines set by federal/state monitoring-frequency rules (tied to population served and source-water type) including an annual July 1 Consumer Confidence Report. A CCR-focused industry source describes missing the certification deadline to the state as 'one of the most common monitoring and reporting violations' and notes penalties escalate from informal notices to formal administrative orders and civil penalties for repeat or serious lapses.
target_customer: Operators of small community water systems (roughly 500-15,000 people served) without in-house compliance staff — the 'system run by one or two operators' segment, not large municipal utilities with their own compliance departments.
evidence: CCR certification misses are described as among the most common SDWA monitoring/reporting violations, with escalating enforcement up to civil penalties (https://www.tapwaterdata.com/regulations/ccr-requirements-2027, fetched 2026-08-19). A concrete penalty example exists: a Tennessee water authority (WWAWC) was fined $1,912 by the state specifically for a missed water-study deadline (https://mainstreetmediatn.com/articles/chronicleofmtjuliet/state-fines-wwawc-1912-for-missed-water-study-deadline/, fetched 2026-08-19). Money already changes hands for compliance help in this exact niche: a commercial competitor, 1water.ai, sells a dedicated tiered-pricing CCR/compliance software product to utilities (referenced from https://www.tapwaterdata.com/regulations/ccr-requirements-2027, fetched 2026-08-19), and rural water associations already charge for related technical assistance — Oklahoma Rural Water Association dues run '$90.00 base, plus $0.90 per connection with a maximum of $4,090.00' (https://orwa.org/system-membership/, fetched 2026-08-19) and National Rural Water Association associate dues are $1,478/yr (https://nrwa.org/members/become-a-member/associate-membership/, fetched 2026-08-19), with California Rural Water Association separately running a fee-based Specialized Utility Services Program on top of membership.
knowledge_base: EPA ECHO's SDWA bulk dataset, confirmed by direct fetch of https://echo.epa.gov/tools/data-downloads (2026-08-19), which lists the live file https://echo.epa.gov/files/echodownloads/SDWA_latest_downloads.zip (457MB) with the page's own stated refresh policy: 'This dataset is updated quarterly.' This dataset covers all ~160,000-170,000 U.S. public water systems' population served, source-water type, and violation/enforcement history nationally. Deadline computation itself comes from a versioned, code-encoded table of the federal Consumer Confidence Report Rule and SDWA monitoring-frequency schedules (40 CFR 141 Subpart O and related tables) applied to each system's own EPA-reported attributes — not scraped or manually curated per customer. Staleness is disclosed directly via an 'as of [EPA quarterly release date]' stamp on every violation-derived claim.
autonomy_case: A1: self-serve signup by PWSID (public water system ID), card payment, automated calendar and email alerts, no onboarding call. A2: code computes each system's next deadlines from its EPA-reported attributes (population served, source type) against a hard-coded federal deadline-rule table, and surfaces any new violation rows appearing in the quarterly SDWA file — a deterministic join and rules evaluation, no manual per-customer curation. A3: when a system's classification data is missing or ambiguous in the federal file, the product says so plainly ('EPA's data doesn't report a source-water type for this PWSID — deadlines below are estimated; confirm with your state primacy agency') instead of guessing silently, and every violation shown links to its source record. A4: EPA's own quarterly-refresh cadence with an explicit staleness stamp; the deadline-rule table is versioned against the published federal regulation, which changes rarely and on a documented Federal Register schedule. A5: quarterly-cron ingest that fails closed with a staleness banner if a scheduled refresh doesn't land. A6: zero human minutes per customer — PWSID lookup and onboarding are self-service, and the federal file already covers essentially all U.S. systems so no bespoke state-specific integration is required for the MVP.
moat: Correctly encoding SDWA's genuinely intricate monitoring-frequency tables (contaminant class x population tier x source type x prior-violation history) is real regulatory grunt work competitors are unlikely to bother doing precisely; once a system's specific deadline calendar lives inside the tool it becomes the operator's system of record with real switching cost.
pricing_hypothesis: $49-$149/mo per system — well under a rural water association's roughly $1,500-$4,000/yr in dues plus fee-based technical-assistance add-ons that partly fund this exact kind of compliance help today.
revenue_model: Monthly per-PWSID self-serve SaaS subscription, card billing.
time_to_first_revenue: 6-8 weeks — the SDWA bulk file is already confirmed live and downloadable; the larger lift is correctly encoding the federal deadline-rule table, which requires more upfront regulatory research than the other two ideas.
risks: The quarterly federal refresh cadence is a real limitation for surfacing 'just happened' violations in near-real-time (mitigated by framing the product primarily around the deadline calendar rather than real-time violation detection); many states layer stricter deadlines on top of the federal floor, so a fully trustworthy product needs per-state rule overlays beyond the federal baseline, which is more domain research than ideas 1-2 require; a named competitor (1water.ai) is already targeting this exact niche, so differentiation on price/narrowness matters.
why_simple: A single national bulk file (already confirmed downloadable) plus a versioned, rarely-changing federal rule table is enough for an MVP — no scraping of 50 heterogeneous state drinking-water portals is required to start, since state-specific overlays can be phase two.

name: TenderGate
one_liner: Self-serve CPV+keyword+country matched daily digest of new EU TED procurement notices for small suppliers, built on TED's live public Search API — no sales call, no analyst.
problem: SMEs bidding for EU/UK public contracts either trawl the raw TED portal manually or pay enterprise-priced, sales-assisted platforms. Stotles' own pricing page (fetched 2026-08-19, https://www.stotles.com/pricing) shows a free tier that quickly gives way to paid tiers from £75-99/mo up to Growth plans from £475-990/mo and Expert 'custom pricing' (i.e., sales call) — evidence that money already changes hands for tender-matching, but the affordable self-serve tier is thin and the valuable tiers require talking to sales.
target_customer: Micro/small firms (5-50 staff) in IT services, construction, translation, facilities management, or consultancy who want a narrow keyword/CPV/country watch on EU public tenders without paying £475+/mo or fielding a sales call.
evidence: Stotles pricing fetched 2026-08-19 (https://www.stotles.com/pricing): free tier limited to tracking + 3 lifetime AI reports, paid tiers £75-990+/mo, top tier is custom/sales-quoted — a materially worse fit (expensive, partly sales-assisted) for a small supplier who just wants a filtered daily list. Secondary corroboration via search (not separately fetched) of Tracker Intelligence at 'from £1,000/year' for UK tender email alerts.
knowledge_base: Official TED (Tenders Electronic Daily) Search API v3: POST https://api.ted.europa.eu/v3/notices/search — verified LIVE by direct fetch on 2026-08-19 (curl POST with a CPV-code query returned real JSON: publication numbers, multilingual notice titles, per-language XML/PDF/HTML links, and totalNoticeCount: 395943). No authentication required for search. Notices carry structured fields (CPV codes, publication date, buyer, deadlines) suitable for deterministic filtering. TED publishes new notices on a rolling daily basis (EU's own procurement portal); staleness is detectable by comparing the max publication-date returned against wall-clock date on each ingestion run.
autonomy_case: A1: signup + Stripe payment + saved-search setup (CPV codes, keywords, countries) all self-serve, no demo. A2: nightly cron POSTs to the TED API, applies deterministic CPV/keyword/date filters, renders a templated digest — pure code, no reviewer. A3: when a notice lacks a structured field (e.g. no published deadline), the digest states 'not published in this notice — see original' rather than inferring one. A4: TED API is the live corpus itself; no scraping or manual curation; a nightly check compares latest ingested publication-date to today to flag pipeline staleness. A5: cron ingestion, Stripe dunning, and a scheduled health-check (alert if TED returns zero new notices for >48h) are all schedulable and fail-closed. A6: support load is bounded — saved searches are self-service CRUD, no bespoke integration is promised.
moat: A growing historical notice archive per buyer/CPV lets the product surface deterministic facts a first-time TED user can't get from a single day's feed (e.g. 'this buyer published N similar notices in the last 24 months') — a compounding data asset, not a content moat.
pricing_hypothesis: $79-249/mo tiered by number of saved searches/CPV watchlists, positioned against Stotles' £475+/mo tiers and £1,000/yr entry-level competitors.
revenue_model: Monthly/annual SaaS subscription, Stripe self-serve checkout and dunning.
time_to_first_revenue: 2-3 weeks (ingestion pipeline against a confirmed-live API + Stripe + templated email digest).
risks: TED itself offers a free notice-search UI, so raw access isn't scarce — value must come entirely from curation UX and reliability of the digest, not from gating access to notices. Not yet verified: whether TED's own free 'my alerts' feature (if any) is good enough to blunt willingness to pay; this needs a follow-up check of TED's own alerting feature before committing.
why_simple: The core product is a cron job that POSTs a structured query to a confirmed-live government API and renders the JSON response into an email template — no model call is needed to produce the customer's paid deliverable.

name: PortfolioWatch UK
one_liner: Nightly diff-and-alert monitoring of Companies House filing deadlines and PSC/officer/status changes across a portfolio of hundreds of UK companies, for accountants and credit teams — built directly on the free, live Companies House API.
problem: Accountants managing many clients, and SME credit/collections teams tracking customers or suppliers, need to know the moment a company's confirmation statement or accounts go overdue, or its PSC/directors/status change (an early distress or change-of-control signal). Red Flag Alert, a paid monitoring tool for exactly this, starts at £200.00/month per Capterra's listing (fetched 2026-08-19, https://www.capterra.co.uk/software/1044714/red-flag-alert) — direct evidence money already changes hands for portfolio-level company monitoring, at a price point far above what a small practice or SME credit team wants to pay for pure alerting.
target_customer: Small accountancy/company-secretarial practices (50-500 client companies) and SME finance/credit teams who need automated overdue-filing and ownership-change alerts across a book of UK companies, without a £200+/mo enterprise monitoring contract.
evidence: Red Flag Alert starting price £200.00 (Capterra UK, fetched 2026-08-19, https://www.capterra.co.uk/software/1044714/red-flag-alert). Adjacent evidence of willingness to pay for Companies-House-derived compliance tooling: Inform Direct's tiered company-secretarial pricing (fetched 2026-08-19, https://www.informdirect.co.uk/business-overview/pricing/) — £10/mo for the first company plus £0.69/company for companies 2-50, scaling down per company at higher volumes — shows practices already pay per-company recurring fees for Companies-House-linked deadline management (Inform Direct additionally files; a pure-monitoring product is a lighter, cheaper adjacent play).
knowledge_base: UK Companies House REST API, base https://api.company-information.service.gov.uk — verified LIVE by direct fetch on 2026-08-19 (unauthenticated request to /company/00000006 returned HTTP 401 'Empty Authorization header', confirming the endpoint is real and requires only a free API key, not a paid one). Rate limit confirmed via Companies House's own developer-specs rate-limiting guide (fetched 2026-08-19, https://developer-specs.company-information.service.gov.uk/guides/rateLimiting): 600 requests per 5-minute window, resetting automatically, with 429s on excess — a documented, generous, free ceiling. Company profile responses include structured confirmation_statement.next_due, accounts.next_due, and company_status fields; PSC endpoints return notified_on/ceased_on dates. Data updates same-day as filings; staleness is detectable by comparing a company's last-seen snapshot date against 'today'.
autonomy_case: A1: self-serve signup, add companies by number or CSV upload, Stripe billing — no onboarding call. A2: nightly cron polls the CH API per watched company, diffs the JSON against the prior snapshot, and emits deterministic alerts (accounts N days overdue, PSC added/removed, status changed to dissolved/liquidation) via a fixed template — no analyst touches any alert. A3: when a field is null (e.g., no accounts filed yet), the alert says 'not yet reported by Companies House' rather than inferring a risk score; the product never asserts a judgment the source data doesn't support. A4: the CH API is the live source of truth with no manual curation; a daily pipeline check flags staleness if no companies' snapshots have changed in an implausible window. A5: nightly ingestion cron, Stripe dunning, and uptime/health-check monitoring are all schedulable and fail-closed. A6: alerts are formulaic diffs — no bespoke integration or human risk review is offered, bounding support load by design.
moat: A time-series of each portfolio company's filing/PSC history becomes a proprietary baseline (e.g., 'this company is usually 3 days late, this time it's 90') that a one-off Companies House lookup can't replicate, and it compounds the longer a customer's portfolio is monitored.
pricing_hypothesis: $49-199/mo tiered by portfolio size (50/250/1,000 companies watched), undercutting Red Flag Alert's £200+/mo entry price for a narrower, monitoring-only feature set.
revenue_model: Monthly SaaS subscription tiered by number of monitored companies.
time_to_first_revenue: 2-3 weeks (CH API integration behind a free key, diff engine, Stripe, templated alert emails).
risks: Companies House itself may offer a free 'follow a company' single-company email alert (not yet verified live) which could blunt appetite for a paid tool at small scale — the wedge has to be portfolio scale (hundreds of companies), structured diffing, and historical baselining, not bare single-company alerts. Also, PSC register updates lag the underlying legal change by up to the statutory notification windows, which the product must state plainly rather than imply real-time.
why_simple: The paid deliverable is a JSON diff between two nightly API snapshots rendered into a template — no generative model is required to produce the alert content.

name: VAT ID Watch
one_liner: Continuous re-validation of customers'/suppliers' EU VAT numbers against the official live VIES register, alerting the moment a number goes invalid so cross-border B2B sellers don't keep zero-rating invoices to a deregistered counterparty.
problem: EU/UK B2B sellers doing reverse-charge or zero-rated intra-EU sales must hold VIES proof of a valid customer VAT number, but that validity can lapse at any time after the initial check — and re-checking manually doesn't scale across an AP/AR book. viesapi.eu, a commercial wrapper around the free official VIES service, sells exactly a paid monitoring layer on top of the free government check: its Professional tier (€40/month, fetched 2026-08-19, https://viesapi.eu/offer/) explicitly adds 'VAT number monitoring' as a paid upgrade over basic on-demand checking — direct evidence that ongoing monitoring, not just single lookups, is what buyers pay extra for.
target_customer: SME finance/AP teams and e-commerce sellers with EU cross-border B2B trade who need their customer/supplier VAT-number master data kept continuously valid for VAT compliance and audit purposes, without building their own SOAP integration and retry logic.
evidence: viesapi.eu pricing (fetched 2026-08-19, https://viesapi.eu/offer/): Startup €8/mo (1,000 requests), Business €24/mo (5,000 requests, recommended), Professional €40/mo (10,000 requests, adds 'VAT number monitoring' and request statistics) — a live, priced commercial product built entirely on top of a free EU government service, proving willingness to pay specifically for the monitoring/tooling layer rather than the underlying check itself.
knowledge_base: Official EU VIES (VAT Information Exchange System) SOAP web service, WSDL at ec.europa.eu/taxation_customs/vies/checkVatService.wsdl — the primary, free, government-run register queried live per VAT number on every call (confirmed via European Commission's own VIES site, fetched 2026-08-19, https://ec.europa.eu/taxation_customs/vies/#/technical-information, and corroborated by the WSDL location surfaced in a live search). Because each check queries the member state's national register in real time, there is no bulk corpus to go stale — staleness is a non-issue by construction, and known VIES downtime is handled by the product marking status 'unknown — retry pending' rather than staling silently.
autonomy_case: A1: self-serve signup, CSV upload or simple API of VAT numbers to watch, Stripe billing, no onboarding call. A2: a scheduled worker re-queries the official VIES SOAP service for every stored VAT number on a fixed cadence and deterministically diffs valid/invalid/name-mismatch state against the last check — the answer comes straight from the government register, no human or model judgment involved. A3: on VIES timeout or unavailability (a documented characteristic of the service), the product reports 'unknown — retry pending' rather than guessing valid/invalid, and retries automatically — genuine self-contained degradation rather than escalation. A4: the corpus is the live government register itself, queried directly, with no scraping or manual curation possible or needed. A5: cron re-checks with backoff/retry on VIES downtime, and monitoring/alerting on the scheduler itself, are fully schedulable and fail-closed. A6: this is a pure API-diffing product — zero human minutes per customer, and support load is bounded because there is no bespoke integration to maintain per customer.
moat: A per-VAT-number historical validity timeline (exact date a customer's VAT ID lapsed) becomes a proprietary audit trail that sellers can hand directly to auditors — something a one-off check can never reconstruct — plus retry/backoff engineering around VIES's well-documented flakiness is real, defensible plumbing work.
pricing_hypothesis: $39-149/mo flat-fee tiers by number of monitored VAT numbers (100/1,000/5,000), positioned as a monitoring-native alternative to viesapi.eu's per-request metered pricing.
revenue_model: Monthly SaaS subscription tiered by watched-VAT-number volume.
time_to_first_revenue: 1-2 weeks (thin SOAP client + scheduler + diff logic + Stripe — the simplest of the three to ship).
risks: The underlying VIES check is free and commoditized — many open-source client libraries exist (confirmed via search: PHP, Python, Java wrappers) — so the product must sell the monitoring/diffing/audit-trail workflow, not access to the check itself, or it has no moat against a customer just self-hosting an open-source wrapper. VIES also has known intermittent downtime/instability that must be engineered around (retry/backoff) rather than papered over.
why_simple: The paid deliverable is a scheduled SOAP call diffed against the last-known state and rendered into an alert — no LLM or generative step is needed anywhere in the fulfilment path.
persona: international/EU public data (EU VIES VAT register)
